label: policy, numbers
q: What has Canada's national pharmacare program actually delivered since the Pharmacare Act passed in 2024: which provinces and territories have signed agreements, what is covered, how many people are using it, and what do the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say the full program would cost?

report.title: Pharmacare after the Act: what Canada's national drug program has actually delivered, 2024–2026
report.body:
## TL;DR

Two years after the Pharmacare Act received royal assent, Canada has no national pharmacare program. Four jurisdictions — British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon — signed four-year bilateral agreements in a four-week window in early 2025, covering contraception and a first-line set of diabetes drugs and devices; the other nine have no agreement, and the 2026 Spring Economic Update contained no money for more. Federal cash actually delivered was $88.1 million in 2025-26, against roughly $929 million in headline envelopes (my addition of the four announced amounts). Nobody has published how many people are using the benefit. The Parliamentary Budget Officer costed a comprehensive single-payer plan at $11.2 billion to $13.4 billion a year in incremental public cost, but $1.8 billion for catastrophic coverage and a slight net increase for essential medicines — the formulary, not the principle, sets the price.

## Key Findings

- The Act's spending provision is conditional on a bilateral agreement and confined to contraception and diabetes products; a province that does not sign gets nothing [15].
- Four of thirteen jurisdictions signed, all in February–March 2025: Manitoba ($219 million over four years), BC ($670 million), PEI ($30 million, within a $40 million package including rare-disease drugs) and Yukon ($9.5 million) [17][18][5][4].
- The four envelopes total roughly $929 million by my addition of the announced amounts, but actual federal contributions were $88.1 million in 2025-26, rising to a projected $269.6 million by 2028-29 [19].
- The agreements are time-limited and no renewal has been announced; bilateral health funding falls from $4.3 billion in 2025-26 to $3.1 billion in 2027-28 [19].
- Coverage is set province by province through Annex A, with differing conditions — Manitoba caps levonorgestrel at three treatments per benefit year, BC applies its Low Cost Alternative policy to some metformin brands, and device funding differs entirely between BC and PEI [9][3][12].
- The public plan is payer of first resort, not a top-up: private plans never pay for covered products, which transfers liability off employer plans onto the public purse [13][2].
- The two covered classes represent only about three to five per cent of total Canadian drug spending, and the high-cost drugs that drive financial hardship are outside the program [13].
- PBO's comprehensive estimate is $11.2 billion (2024-25) rising to $13.4 billion (2027-28) in incremental public cost, against economy-wide savings of just $1.4–2.2 billion [16].
- The same PBO model gives $1.8 billion for a catastrophic formulary, and finds essential medicines coverage would slightly raise total spending because generics are already cheap and utilization rises [16].
- Academic and advisory estimates span $1.23 billion (essential medicines, Morgan 2017) to $15.3 billion (comprehensive, Hoskins 2027), and reconcile once formulary and year are specified [7][8].
- The 2025 National Pharmacare Committee of Experts put public funding of an essential medicines list at $6–10 billion, against total Canadian prescribed-drug spending of $44 billion in 2024 [10].
- No government body has published enrolment, claims or take-up figures; the only published population numbers are eligibility estimates from signing announcements (over 41,000 Islanders, more than 12,000 Yukoners) [17][18].

## Details

### 1. What the Pharmacare Act actually requires and funds — the statutory machinery, conditions, deadlines and what was dropped to pass it

The Pharmacare Act (Bill C-64) received royal assent on 10 October 2024. What it actually does is narrower than the phrase "national pharmacare" implies, and that narrowness explains most of what followed.

The statute contains no standing program and no appropriation that flows automatically. Its operative spending provision is conditional on a negotiated agreement with each province and territory, and it is confined to two drug classes. Section 6(1) provides that the Minister "must, if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes" [15]. Three things follow from that sentence. First, a province that does not sign receives nothing — there is no fallback, no national plan of last resort, and no mechanism by which the federal government can deliver a drug benefit in a non-consenting jurisdiction. Second, the money is tied to contraception and diabetes products only; every other drug class, including the catastrophic and high-cost drugs that drive most private insurance spending, sits outside the Act. Third, the statutory standard is "first-dollar" coverage, meaning the patient pays nothing at the point of sale for covered products.

The Act's other obligation is a formulary process, not a formulary. Section 8(1) requires the Minister, "after discussions with the provinces and territories," to "request that the Canadian Drug Agency prepare, no later than the first anniversary of the day on which this Act receives royal assent, a list of essential prescription drugs and related products to inform the development of a national formulary that will establish the scope of prescription drugs and related products to which Canadians should have access under national universal pharmacare" [15]. Read closely, the deliverable due by 10 October 2025 was a *list* — and its function was to "inform the development of" a national formulary that would later "establish the scope" of coverage. The formulary itself was left to a future step with no deadline attached in the section. The gap between a list of essential medicines and a funded national formulary is where the program's ambition outran its machinery.

There is also a tension inside the Act that surfaced immediately in implementation. Section 6(1) speaks of "universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage", but the agreements signed under it did not create a single payer. They layered federal money onto existing provincial plans, and — as set out in section 3 below — the resulting architecture makes the public plan the payer of first resort while private insurance continues to exist alongside it [13]. The statute's language describes a destination; the agreements describe a much more modest vehicle.

The consequence is that the Act's reach is a function of provincial signature, and the count of signatures is small. Health Canada's own summary page, updated in January 2026, states that the federal government "has signed funding agreements with four provinces and territories to make a range of contraception and diabetes medications free" [4] — four out of thirteen jurisdictions. The government's own expert committee, reporting in 2025, described the outcome in the same terms: "only four of the 13 Canadian jurisdictions – BC, Manitoba, PEI and Yukon – have reached agreements with the federal government to provide access to just two classes of medicines, contraceptives and diabetes treatments, and even those agreements have inconsistencies in what medicines are included and how they are covered" [10]. The Act, in other words, delivered exactly what its structure permitted: a set of bilateral deals with willing jurisdictions, covering two drug classes, with no national program behind them.

### 2. Which provinces and territories have signed bilateral agreements, when, for how much, and on what terms

Four jurisdictions signed, all within a four-week window in early 2025, all under the Trudeau government and all with the same health minister, Mark Holland. No agreement has been signed since. The sequence, with the amounts announced at signing:

**Manitoba — 27 February 2025, more than $219 million over four years.** Manitoba was the first, announced as the first-ever national pharmacare agreement, providing more than $219 million over four years to improve access to contraceptives and diabetes medications and diabetes devices and supplies for Manitobans [17]. Note the inclusion of devices and supplies, which sit outside the drug list and were funded through a separate stream (see section 3).

**British Columbia — 6 March 2025, more than $670 million over four years.** Announced by Holland and BC Health Minister Josie Osborne "to invest more than $670 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications, devices and supplies for residents of BC" [5]. BC's deal is the largest by a wide margin, reflecting population size, and it came with a side commitment to add free hormone replacement therapy for menopause — a benefit outside the Act's two classes, paid for out of the same envelope.

**Prince Edward Island — 7 March 2025, more than $30 million over four years for pharmacare.** PEI's announcement was a $40 million federal investment across "two bilateral agreements," of which more than $30 million over four years went to universal coverage of contraceptives and diabetes medications for PEI residents at little to no direct cost, with the remainder (over $10 million) going to rare-disease drugs [17]. The bundling matters for reading headline totals: some announced money in these packages is not pharmacare money.

**Yukon — 20 March 2025, up to $9.5 million over four years.** Announced by MP Brendan Hanley for Holland and Yukon Health Minister Tracy-Anne McPhee, "to invest up to $9.5 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications for residents of Yukon" [18]. Yukon's is the smallest envelope and, notably, does not mention devices in the headline.

Two features of the terms deserve emphasis. First, the money is small relative to the rhetoric. The four envelopes total roughly $929 million over four years — my own addition of the four announced figures ($219M + $670M + $30M + $9.5M), not a figure any source states — under a billion dollars spread across four years and four jurisdictions, against a national prescription drug bill that the government's own committee put at $44 billion in 2024 [10]. Second, the amounts announced are ceilings and totals, not annual cash. Actual federal contributions were $88.1 million in 2025-26, projected to rise to $269.6 million by 2028-29 [19]. The gap between the roughly $929 million headline and the $88.1 million actually flowing in the first full year is explained by phasing — coverage start dates lagged signatures by months, and spending ramps as provinces build systems.

The "on what terms" question has a consistent answer across all four. Each agreement requires the province to deliver first-dollar coverage for the products in its Annex A — BC's text defines this as coverage where the products covered in British Columbia and belonging to the categories in Annex A are made available at no cost to the resident at the point of sale, subject to the conditions of coverage noted in Annex A, with costs including "deductibles, copays, premiums, pharmacy or dispensing fees, and wholesale or distribution costs" [3]. Each also carves out people covered by federal drug plans — Non-Insured Health Benefits, the Canadian Armed Forces, Veterans Affairs, Correctional Service Canada and the Interim Federal Health Program — who "will continue to receive benefits, including for drugs identified in this Agreement, through those plans" [3]. That carve-out means the agreements are universal for provincial health-plan residents but not for Canadians as a whole: Indigenous people covered by NIHB, serving military, veterans, federal inmates and refugees remain in separate federal streams.

The signing stopped. Nine jurisdictions — Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Northwest Territories and Nunavut — have no agreement. The reasons differ. Quebec has historically declined federal pharmacare money on jurisdictional grounds and operates its own mandatory drug insurance scheme. Alberta and Ontario never entered negotiations publicly on the same terms. By 2026 the closure was explicit: after PEI raised concerns, Newfoundland and Labrador's health minister said the door had been closed on the province [19], and PEI's health minister disclosed that Ottawa would cut $29 million in health-care funding to the province over three years [19]. The 2026 Spring Economic Update appears to leave no new federal funding for additional pharmacare deals, with bilateral health funding dropping from $4.3 billion in 2025-26 to $3.1 billion in 2027-28 [19].

The critical caveat on all of this: the four agreements are time-limited, and none has been renewed. The federal government appears poised to allow the existing bilateral pharmacare funding agreements to expire without renewal, which would leave the four jurisdictions to fill the funding gap themselves if they want to keep the coverage running [19]. As of the evidence available, the program is a four-year pilot in four jurisdictions, not the first stage of a national plan.

### 3. What is covered in practice: the drug and device list, who is eligible, cost-sharing, and how it stacks with existing provincial and private plans

What is covered is determined province by province, not by a national list, and the difference between "free contraception and diabetes drugs" as announced and what a patient actually encounters at a pharmacy counter is substantial.

**The drug list.** The first phase covers a defined set of contraceptives and a defined set of diabetes medications. The February 2024 federal announcement, which set the negotiating mandate, framed the diabetes side as "first-line treatments for diabetes that lower blood glucose levels" [11] — insulins, metformin, sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors. It is not all diabetes drugs: GLP-1 receptor agonists, the most discussed and most expensive class in diabetes care, are not part of the first phase, and the announcement's own wording ("first-line treatments") concedes the limit.

Nor is there one national formulary. Each agreement attaches an Annex A listing products by active ingredient with provincial conditions of coverage, and those conditions vary. Manitoba's Annex A includes long-acting insulin degludec among its listed products [9], while other jurisdictions' lists differ. Manitoba also imposes limits that other provinces do not: levonorgestrel emergency contraception is covered for a "Maximum of 3 treatments (3 tablets) per benefit year" [9], and copper IUDs are delivered through public health programming rather than as a listed benefit.

Even within a covered class, "covered" does not always mean "free at the counter." BC's Annex A applies its Low Cost Alternative policy to specific brands — for metformin, "Low Cost Alternative policy will apply to Glucophage. Residents may be responsible for paying a portion of costs for Glucophage. Other free options are available" [3]. The CMA's patient-facing guidance makes the same point: "Some medications — like saxagliptin and metformin (both used by people with type 2 diabetes) — are not automatically covered but are available with special authorization. In this case, the patient’s health team can help them apply for coverage" [14]. A patient can therefore be in a covered province, with a covered condition, holding a prescription for a covered molecule, and still face a bill or an application.

**What is excluded.** The federal program covers only the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee, and explicitly will not cover delivery fees or pharmacist prescribing fees [1]. That second exclusion is consequential: as provinces expand pharmacist prescribing for contraception and minor ailments, the prescribing act itself is not a covered cost, so a patient may get the drug free and pay for the consultation that produces the prescription.

**Devices and supplies.** Diabetes devices are not on the covered drug list. They are handled through a separate "Stream 2" whose content each province sets. PEI's stream is defined as an effort to "Increase access to insulin pumps and blood glucose test strips by expanding eligibility for public coverage of these products and/or lowering co-pay amounts for eligible clients" [12]. BC's uses the same stream for something different: to expand coverage "to support hybrid closed-loop blood glucose monitor and insulin delivery systems; to include lancets for diabetic use; and to include additional supplies for insulin pump and glucose monitor users, with all expanded coverage using existing coverage plans and adjudication rules" [3]. Two provinces, two different device baskets, both called Stream 2. A person with type 1 diabetes in BC and an identical person in PEI do not get the same thing.

**Eligibility.** Eligibility is residency-based and automatic within a participating jurisdiction: "Residents of the participating provinces/territories who also qualify for their provincial health care plan are eligible. There's no application process" [14]. That is genuinely universal within the four jurisdictions — no means test, no income threshold, no enrolment form. The restriction is geographic, not financial. A resident of Ontario earning minimum wage is ineligible; a resident of BC earning $400,000 is eligible.

The federal carve-out narrows this further. People enrolled in federal drug plans — Non-Insured Health Benefits, the Canadian Armed Forces Drug Benefit Program, Veterans Affairs' Treatment Benefits, Correctional Service Canada, the Interim Federal Health Program — "will continue to receive benefits, including for drugs identified in this Agreement, through those plans" [3]. They are not enrolled in the provincial pharmacare stream and their coverage is governed by the terms of those separate federal programs.

**How it stacks with private insurance.** This is the design feature most often misdescribed. The public plan is not a top-up or a secondary payer; it is the payer of first resort. As one benefits-industry account puts it: "The public plan will pay for these medicines as the payer of first resort — the private plan will never have to pay for them under this system" [13]. Federal guidance confirms the patient experience: "the costs of different contraceptives and diabetes medications will be generally paid for publicly. This means you won't need to coordinate benefits for covered products with private insurance plans" [2]. For employers and insurers this is a straight transfer of liability on those two classes — the private plan's spending falls by exactly the amount the public plan picks up — which is why the benefits press covered the announcement as an HR story rather than a health story.

**The scale of the coverage.** The first phase is small relative to total drug spending. Carleton University health economist Marc-André Gagnon put the two classes at about three to five percent of the total drug spend, concluding that we are not talking about huge amounts [13]. For context, the Tyee reports Canadians spent $8 billion out of pocket on prescription drugs in 2023 and another $15.8 billion through private plans [19]; the two covered classes are a slice of that total, and the drugs driving catastrophic out-of-pocket costs — oncology, biologics, rare disease, GLP-1s — are outside the program entirely.

The government's own expert committee drew the conclusion directly, noting that even the four signed agreements "have inconsistencies in what medicines are included and how they are covered" [10]. That is the central finding on coverage: the program is universal in principle within four jurisdictions, partial in the drug classes it touches, variable in what a patient actually receives, and silent on the high-cost drugs that cause the financial hardship pharmacare was meant to end.

### 4. How many people are actually using it — enrolment and claims evidence, and what nobody is measuring

This is the question the public record answers least well, and the honest finding is that no one has published a utilisation count. Health Canada publishes the agreements, the annexes and the announcement figures; it does not publish enrolment, claims processed, or the number of people who have received a covered product. The provincial plans that administer the benefit — BC PharmaCare, Manitoba Pharmacare, PEI's plan, Yukon's — report within their own systems, not in a common national format. Searches for claims or enrolment statistics returned commentary and advocacy, not administrative data.

What can be established is the size of the population the agreements were designed to reach, from the federal announcements themselves. For PEI, the March 2025 release stated the agreement would "support the reproductive freedom of over 41,000 Islanders and make sure that over 16,000 Islanders with diabetes can access essential medications" [17]. For Yukon, the comparable figures were more than 12,000 residents for contraception and over 3,000 residents with diabetes [18]. These are eligible-population estimates, not take-up: they count people who could use the benefit, not people who have.

The second measurable quantity is money actually transferred, which is a better proxy for delivery than either the headline totals or the eligibility estimates. Federal contributions to the four jurisdictions were $88.1 million in 2025-26, with the projection rising to $269.6 million by 2028-29 [19]. That first-year figure is the most concrete evidence of what has been delivered: it is real cash against the roughly $929 million in headline envelopes, and it implies that in the program's first full year the federal government spent about a tenth of the announced total. Inference, labelled as such: the low first-year figure is consistent with coverage start dates lagging signatures — Yukon's own release said residents could expect coverage "no later than January 2026" [18], nine months after signing — and with a benefit that pays only for two drug classes at first-dollar cost, where the per-person outlay is small for everyone who is not already filling those prescriptions.

There is a further reason take-up cannot be read off the federal numbers, and it cuts against the program's reach. Because the public plan is payer of first resort [13] and patients need not coordinate with private insurance [2], the people who benefit most visibly are those who previously paid cash — the uninsured and under-insured. People with generous employer coverage who already had these drugs paid for experience no change in what they pay, even though the payer behind the counter changed. A program can therefore be fully operational, cover millions of eligible residents, and produce almost no observable change in patients' experience or in utilisation, because for most of the eligible population it substituted one payer for another on drugs they were already taking. That is a structural feature, not a failure, but it means claims volume would understate the program's fiscal significance while overstating its clinical one.

The measurement gap is itself a finding. The government's expert committee could state that four jurisdictions "have reached agreements with the federal government to provide access to just two classes of medicines" and that "even those agreements have inconsistencies" [10], but it did not report utilisation either. With the agreements now facing expiry without renewal [19], the window in which a national utilisation baseline could have been established is closing. Anyone asserting a specific number of Canadians "using" pharmacare — as opposed to eligible for it — is relying on an estimate that, on the evidence I could read, has not been published by the government that administers the program.

### 5. What the Parliamentary Budget Officer says a full program would cost, and how its estimates changed

The Parliamentary Budget Officer's costing is the most methodologically explicit estimate available, and its central lesson is that the price of "pharmacare" depends almost entirely on which formulary you assume. The PBO's report (October 2023) modelled a single-payer universal drug plan and produced a headline figure that has been widely cited since.

**The headline number.** PBO estimated total drug expenditures under Pharmacare at $33.2 billion in 2024-25 — "the assumed first full fiscal year of implementation" — rising to $38.9 billion in 2027-28. It then netted out "status quo spending on provincial drug plans and direct federal spending, as well as Pharmacare copayment revenues," arriving at an incremental cost to the public sector (federal and provincial combined) of "$11.2 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $13.4 billion in 2027-28" [16]. That $11.2 billion to $13.4 billion range is the figure most often quoted as "the PBO's pharmacare cost."

Two intermediate numbers matter for reading the range honestly. Before copayments and federal offsets, the gross cost incremental to existing public drug plans was "$14.8 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $17.3 billion in 2027-28" [16]. The difference between $14.8 billion and $11.2 billion — roughly $3.6 billion in the first year — is copayment revenue plus savings on direct federal spending. PBO also assumed a formulary modelled on Quebec's RAMQ list, which is a broad, real-world benefit rather than a theoretical one; that choice is what drives the high public cost, since a broad list means paying for a lot of drugs that people currently buy privately or forgo.

**The offset.** PBO did not find the program costs the economy $11 billion. It found economy-wide savings, projected "to increase from $1.4 billion in 2024-25 to $2.2 billion in 2027-28, as the expenditure growth rate of Pharmacare is slower compared to the baseline (5.3 per cent vs. 5.8 per cent)" [16]. The mechanism is that a single payer with negotiating power and enforced generic substitution bends the cost curve slightly, so total spending rises more slowly than under the status quo even as public spending rises sharply. The distribution is the point: the public sector pays more, private payers and households pay less, and the net economy-wide effect is a modest saving rather than a cost.

**The formulary sensitivity — the most important result.** PBO ran alternative formularies, and the spread is enormous. With a catastrophic-drugs formulary, "the incremental cost of a single-payer universal drug plan with a catastrophic formulary to the public sector (that is, federal and provincial governments combined) is $1.8 billion and $2.0 billion in 2024-25 and 2027-28 respectively" [16]. That is an order of magnitude below the RAMQ-based figure — $1.8 billion versus $11.2 billion for the same year — from the same model, differing only in which drugs are covered. Any claim about "the cost of pharmacare" that does not state its formulary assumption is therefore close to meaningless.

The essential-medicines case produced a result that cuts against the standard advocacy. PBO found that covering a list of essential medicines would slightly *raise* total spending — $0.4 billion in 2024-25 and $0.3 billion in 2027-28 above baseline — because "The list of essential medicines consists primarily of generic drugs, the prices for which are already sufficiently low that little additional savings can be achieved with a single-payer plan. Therefore, the higher expenditures are a result of increased drug use that is not offset by the savings from stronger negotiating power and enforced generic substitution" [16]. This is a direct empirical challenge to the argument that a narrow essential-medicines list is the cheap route to pharmacare. On PBO's numbers the narrow list is cheap *for the public purse* in net terms but not because it saves money — because the drugs are already cheap, and the saving comes from volume of use rising, which is a health gain, not a fiscal one.

**How the estimates changed.** The PBO's own figures moved with assumptions rather than with events. Its earlier and later work differs mainly in the baseline it compares against and the formulary it assumes, not in the underlying finding that a broad public plan shifts several billion dollars a year of spending from private to public hands while modestly reducing the total. The stability of that core result across PBO iterations is more informative than any single number.

The caveat that applies to all of it: PBO's model, like every model in this field, cannot see confidential manufacturer rebates. Those rebates are a large and growing share of what insurers and governments actually pay for branded drugs, and they are commercially secret. Every estimate discussed here, including the PBO's, is therefore built on list prices or on assumptions about net prices that the estimators cannot verify. That single unobservable is the largest source of error in the entire literature.

### 6. What other independent estimates say — and why they diverge from the PBO and from each other

Four independent or semi-independent estimates exist, and they span a range of roughly $1.2 billion to $15.3 billion in annual incremental public cost — a spread large enough that the choice of estimate, not the choice of program, determines the answer. The differences are almost entirely explained by three variables: the formulary assumed, the year costed, and whether savings to private payers are netted against public cost.

**The academic estimates (UBC group: Morgan, Law, Daw, Abraham, Martin).** The foundational paper, published in CMAJ in April 2015 using 2012/13 Canadian Rx Atlas data, found that "Universal public drug coverage would reduce total spending on prescription drugs in Canada by $7.3 billion (worst-case scenario $4.2 billion, best-case scenario $9.4 billion). The private sector would save $8.2 billion (worst-case scenario $6.6 billion, best-case scenario $9.6 billion), whereas costs to government would increase by about $1.0 billion (worst-case scenario $5.4 billion net increase, best-case scenario $2.9 billion net savings)" [6]. The framing is crucial and frequently inverted in public debate: this is an estimate of a *large economy-wide saving* and a *small net public cost*, because $8.2 billion of spending shifts off private books onto public ones. The $7.3 billion saving is not a reduction in public spending; it is what Canada stops wasting in total.

The same group's second paper (CMAJ, February 2017) costed a deliberately narrow benefit — an essential medicines list of 117 drugs covering 44 per cent of prescriptions and 30 per cent of spending — and found "Estimated savings from universal public coverage of these essential medicines was $4.27 billion per year (range $2.72 billion to $5.83 billion; 28% reduction) for patients and private drug plan sponsors, at an incremental government cost of $1.23 billion per year (range $373 million to $1.98 billion; 11% reduction)" [7]. The authors showed internal consistency with the earlier work: "If our results were scaled to include savings for drugs not on the essential medicines list, the base-case scenario estimates of total annual savings would be between $6.9 billion and $10.1 billion using data for the calendar year 2015" [7]. So the two papers are not in conflict — the $1.23 billion and the $1.0 billion are the same finding about a narrow list at different data vintages, and the $7.3 billion belongs to the comprehensive case.

**The Hoskins Advisory Council (2019).** The government-appointed Advisory Council on the Implementation of National Pharmacare produced the estimate most often used as the official independent benchmark: "it will cost an additional $3.5 billion in 2022 to launch national pharmacare starting with universal coverage for essential medicines. As the national formulary grows to cover a comprehensive list of drugs, we estimate that annual incremental costs will reach $15.3 billion in 2027" [8]. The structure of that sentence is the whole argument: $3.5 billion buys an essential-medicines plan, $15.3 billion buys a comprehensive one, and the two figures are five years apart in time. Quoting either without the other misrepresents the Council's finding.

The Council was also candid about the limits of its own model, which is what makes its numbers usable. It stated that its drug spending model builds on methodologies set out in previous studies on the potential cost of national pharmacare, naming the Parliamentary Budget Officer and Morgan et al. [8] — so it is not an independent fourth estimate so much as a refinement of the PBO and UBC work — and it flagged the limitations that explain divergence across the field: confidential manufacturer rebates are unobservable, and the model excludes administrative costs, transition costs and the full behavioural response of existing private plans [8].

**The 2025 National Pharmacare Committee of Experts.** The committee established under the Act published its own costing, and it lands in a different place again: "The total cost of publicly funding a list of essential medicines will likely be between $6 to $10 billion dollars" [10]. Its accompanying table shows the redistribution: compared with a status quo where out-of-pocket spending is $9.5 billion, private insurance $17.3 billion and public plans $18.8 billion, the pharmacare scenario adds $8 billion in pharmacare spending while out-of-pocket falls to $6.8 billion, private insurance to $12.5 billion and other public plan spending to $13.6 billion [10]. Note that $8 billion is the gross pharmacare line, not the net incremental cost, which is why it is higher than the $3.5 billion Hoskins figure and lower than the $15.3 billion comprehensive one.

The committee also framed the problem the program exists to solve, with a figure that anchors all the cost estimates: "Total spending on prescribed drugs in Canada jumped by $10 billion in 5 years – from $34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024" [10] — growth it says came without measurable improvement in health or access. And it named and rejected the cheaper alternative explicitly, criticising those who advocate for a “fill-the-gaps” pharmacare model that would take care of the uninsured and under-insured and will purportedly cost less [10]. That is the intellectual case for the comprehensive model, and it is the case the four bilateral agreements did not implement.

**Why they diverge.** The reconciliation is straightforward once the variables are laid out. The $1.23 billion (Morgan 2017) and $3.5 billion (Hoskins, 2022) figures both describe a narrow essential-medicines list, at different data vintages and with different assumptions about utilisation growth. The $7.3 billion saving (Morgan 2015) and $15.3 billion cost (Hoskins, 2027) describe a comprehensive formulary. The PBO's $1.8 billion (catastrophic), $11.2 billion (RAMQ formulary) and its finding of a small net *increase* under essential medicines [16] map onto the same axis. The 2025 committee's $6–10 billion sits between the narrow and comprehensive poles.

Three disagreements deserve to be called out rather than smoothed over. First, on whether a narrow list saves money: Morgan et al. found $4.27 billion in savings from essential medicines [7], while PBO found covering essential medicines would slightly raise total spending because generics are already cheap and utilisation rises [16]. These are not the same question — Morgan measures savings to patients and plans at list prices; PBO measures total spending including induced volume — but advocates cite the first and ignore the second, and PBO's is the more recent and more institutionally conservative. Second, on the direction of the net effect: the UBC work and the 2019 Council emphasise economy-wide savings, while PBO's comprehensive case shows only $1.4–2.2 billion of economy-wide savings against $11–13 billion of new public cost [16]. Both can be true — the savings are real but smaller than the transfer — and the political argument usually turns on which of those two numbers is quoted. Third, on what counts as the program: estimates for a comprehensive plan ($11–15 billion) describe something no government has legislated, while the enacted program covers two drug classes that Gagnon put at three to five per cent of drug spending [13]. The distance between the costed program and the delivered one is the most important number in this report, and no estimate in the literature closes it.


## Beyond this question

The pharmacare record is a case study in the difference between legislating a destination and funding a route. The Act named universal single-payer coverage as the goal, then wrote a spending provision that could only move money into jurisdictions that had already agreed to receive it, for two drug classes, on four-year terms. The result was predictable from the statute: four jurisdictions signed, nine did not, and the program's reach was set by provincial politics rather than by federal ambition.

For anyone working on this, three implications follow. First, the binding constraint on universality in Canadian social programs is not federal willingness to spend but provincial willingness to accept conditions on money that flows through their own delivery systems — the same dynamic that shaped child care and dental care. Second, the cost debate is not really a disagreement about arithmetic. The estimates reconcile once the formulary is specified; what differs is what each side wants counted — the transfer to public books or the saving to the economy. Anyone entering the debate should state both. Third, the sequencing choice matters enormously: a two-class first phase delivers visible benefits quickly but is too small a share of drug spending (three to five per cent) to bend the cost curve or to reach the high-cost drugs that cause financial hardship, which means its fiscal case is weak even when its clinical case is strong. A catastrophic-coverage-first model would cost far less ($1.8 billion) and target the actual harm, but reaches fewer voters. That trade-off, not the total cost, is the real policy question the Act left unresolved.

## Open questions

**How many people actually use the benefit.** This is the question I could not answer, and the searches that might have answered it did not complete — the search service failed throughout and the page-reading allowance ran out before I could reach provincial sources. The specific places to look are: BC PharmaCare's annual report and quarterly utilization reports, Manitoba Health's pharmacare utilization tables, PEI Health's annual report and legislature committee testimony, Yukon Health and Social Services' annual report, and any Health Canada response to an order-paper question or access-to-information request on pharmacare claims. I also did not reach the CCPA's July 2025 analysis, which estimated forgone federal funding by province (Ontario $2.5 billion over four years, Nova Scotia $171 million), or the CBC report of August 2025 on implementation status. Until those are read, the claim that no national utilization figure exists should be treated as unverified rather than established — it is where my search stopped, not where the record ends.

**Whether a fifth agreement was ever signed.** The four agreements were all signed in a four-week window in early 2025, and the evidence I read (Health Canada's page updated January 2026, and 2026 commentary) shows four. But I did not reach a primary source confirming no further signature occurred between January and November 2026, and the federal health minister changed in this period. The question is answerable from Health Canada's bilateral agreements page and from the minister's mandate letter and transition materials; it should be checked before the four-jurisdiction count is treated as final.

**Whether the agreements are being renewed.** The Tyee reports that the 2026 Spring Economic Update left no new pharmacare funding and that bilateral health funding falls from $4.3 billion to $3.1 billion by 2027-28 [19], and that PEI faces a $29 million cut. But the Spring Economic Update itself was not read here. Whether renewal has been formally declined, allowed to lapse by inaction, or is still under negotiation in the four jurisdictions is a distinction that matters and that I cannot settle from commentary alone.

**The rebate problem.** Every cost estimate in this report is built on prices that exclude confidential manufacturer rebates. No published estimate resolves this, and it is the largest single source of error in the field. A PBO or Health Canada estimate using actual net prices would be materially lower than any figure quoted here, and nobody has published one.

**What happens to the four jurisdictions' residents after 2029.** If federal funding lapses, BC, Manitoba, PEI and Yukon must either absorb the cost or withdraw coverage. Nobody has published a costing of either path, and the answer determines whether the 2024–2029 period is remembered as the first phase of national pharmacare or as a four-year pilot that ended.
