q: What does the evidence say about school smartphone bans: which jurisdictions (Ontario, England, the Netherlands, Australian states and others) have adopted them, what have evaluations measured about learning, attention, bullying and mental health, and how strong is that evidence?

report.title: School smartphone bans: what jurisdictions have done, what evaluations measured, and how strong the evidence is
report.body:
## TL;DR

At least 31% of countries and about 30 US states had school phone bans or restrictions by 2024–25, but the policies differ so much in legal force, time coverage and enforcement that "ban" is not one treatment [3]. Where evaluations measure the implementers' opinions — the Netherlands, New South Wales, South Australia — large majorities report improved concentration and learning [15][16]; where studies measure outcomes against a counterfactual, the effects are small or absent. The best-powered study, a pre-registered national US evaluation of lockable pouches across more than 43,000 schools, found effects on test scores "consistently close to zero", no change in attendance, attention or perceived cyberbullying, a rise in disciplinary incidents and a temporary fall in wellbeing that reversed by the third year [8][18]. The evidence supports saying that bans reliably reduce in-school phone use and do not reliably improve achievement, attention, bullying or mental health; it does not support saying bans are useless.

## Key Findings

- **Adoption is near-universal among the jurisdictions usually named, but the instruments are not comparable.** Ontario's PPM 128 (27 June 2024, effective 1 September 2024) restricts use during instructional time only, replacing a 2019 memorandum, and separately requires social media to be blocked on school networks [1]. England's guidance (19 February 2024) covers the whole school day including breaks and lunch but was non-statutory until 29 June 2026 [5][6]. The Netherlands' arrangement is a national agreement implemented school by school since January 2024 [2]. NSW banned phones in public high schools from Term 4 2023 across class, recess and lunch, leaving enforcement method to schools [7]. Florida's HB 379 took effect 1 July 2023 for instructional time [3].

- **Globally, one-quarter of countries had banned phones in schools by 2023, rising to 31% in 2024; 30 US states had statewide bans or recommendations by September 2025** [3].

- **The official evaluations measure beliefs, not outcomes.** The Dutch government-commissioned study surveyed 317 secondary school leaders: 75% said concentration improved, 59% the social environment, 28% that results improved [15]. NSW's survey of almost 1,000 principals found 95% still supported the ban, 81% said learning improved, 87% believed students were less distracted [16]. Neither had a comparison group, baseline or standardised outcome.

- **The largest and most rigorous study finds achievement effects close to zero.** The pre-registered national US pouch study can "rule out improvements larger than approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations" over three years [8]. Its one significant positive result — high-school maths at about 0.024 SD, roughly 0.9 percentile points — is about one-fifth the gain from a higher value-added teacher [8].

- **The achievement literature contains an unresolved direct contradiction.** Beland and Murphy found English exam gains of about 0.07 SD concentrated among the lowest-achieving students [10]; Kessel, Hardardottir and Tyrefors replicated the design on Swedish data and found no effect, able to reject even small gains [12]. Beland and Murphy's survey had a 21% response rate; the replication achieved about 75% by simplifying it [12].

- **Effects, where they appear, arrive late.** Florida's test-score gains were absent in year one, "when disciplinary rates were high", and appeared in year two at 1.1 percentiles on spring tests, larger for male students (1.4) and middle/high-school students (1.3) [3][4].

- **Attention: teachers report large improvements, measured attention does not move.** The pouch study's estimate for classroom attention is -0.088 (SE = 0.085), "no evidence of changes following adoption" [8] — despite in-class personal phone use falling from 61% to 13% [8]. SMART Schools found no difference in teacher-reported classroom disruptiveness between restrictive and permissive English schools [20].

- **Bans create disciplinary work before they reduce it.** Adoption raised the disciplinary index by 0.057 school-level SD (SE = 0.023), about 11%, concentrated in the adoption year and fading thereafter [8].

- **Mental health: the strongest designs find nothing.** Iceland's nationwide difference-in-differences across 70 schools and 23,938 observations found no meaningful change in depressive symptoms, anxiety, hostility or wellbeing, with bullying results similar [21]. SMART Schools found no difference in wellbeing (adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62) against a 3-point minimum clinically important difference [20].

- **The mechanism is displacement, not reduction.** Restrictive English schools had 0.67 fewer hours of phone use and 0.54 fewer hours of social media during school time, but "no evidence for differences when comparing usage time on weekdays or weekends" [20]. Against 4–6 hours of daily phone use, the in-school reduction was too small to shift outcomes [17].

- **Bullying evidence is mixed and measures are not comparable.** The US pouch study found no change in perceived likelihood of online bullying (-0.039, SE = 0.092) [8]; Iceland found no change [21]; King et al. found bullying falling in both ban and no-ban South Australian schools [22]. Against these, Abrahamsson's Norwegian study reports reduced bullying and reduced mental health care use among girls, with academic gains concentrated among lower-SES girls [21].

- **The field cannot support a systematic review.** The LSE/5Rights review reports that "insufficient sources met the quality threshold for inclusion" [9]; Campbell et al.'s scoping review of 22 studies found no randomised controlled trials and incompatible definitions and outcomes [13].

- **No jurisdiction has published an outcome evaluation of its own ban using administrative data.** Ontario has restricted phones since 2019 and tightened the rule in 2024 with no published outcome evaluation [1]; England's guidance became statutory only in June 2026 [6]; the Dutch and NSW evaluations are surveys of school leaders [15][16].

## Details

### 1. 1. Which jurisdictions have adopted school smartphone bans, and what exactly do the rules cover?

The first thing to establish is that "school smartphone ban" is not one policy. The jurisdictions most often named — Ontario, England, the Netherlands, the Australian states, Florida — have adopted instruments of different legal force, covering different times of day, with different exemptions and different enforcement. Most of the disagreement about "whether bans work" is really disagreement about which of these things is being evaluated.

**Ontario.** The operative document is Policy/Program Memorandum 128, issued 27 June 2024 and effective 1 September 2024, under the provincial Code of Conduct [1]. It replaced an earlier PPM 128 dated 29 August 2019, so Ontario's first restriction predates the 2024 headline by five years and was tightened rather than created [1]. The rule is not a blanket prohibition: students must not use personal mobile devices during instructional time except for educational purposes as directed by an educator, for health and medical purposes, and to support special education needs [1]. "Personal mobile device" is defined broadly — "any personal electronic device that can be used to communicate or to access the Internet, such as a cellphone, tablet, laptop or smartwatch" [1] — which means the rule reaches laptops and watches, not just phones.

Two features of the Ontario design matter for interpreting any evaluation. First, the restriction is tied to instructional time, not the school day: grades 7 to 12 must have devices "stored out of view and powered off or set to silent mode during instructional time", while younger pupils (grade 6 and below) must do so for the full instructional day, and non-compliance means handing the device in [1]. Breaks and lunch are outside the prohibition for secondary students. Second, Ontario paired the device rule with a network rule: "School boards are required to restrict access to all social media platforms on school networks and school devices" [1]. That is a second, separate intervention running in parallel, which makes attributing any change to the phone rule alone difficult.

**England.** The Department for Education's guidance, published 19 February 2024, is broader in scope than Ontario's. It "provides statutory guidance to individual schools and trusts on how to implement a policy that prohibits the use of mobile phones throughout the school day, including during lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime" [5]. But it prescribes no method: "There are a number of ways in which schools can ensure that they are mobile phone-free, and it is for headteachers to decide how best to achieve this within their own unique contexts" [5]. Exceptions for disabled pupils and medical needs are built in [5].

The legal status changed late. The guidance was non-statutory for its first two and a half years: revised guidance was published in January 2026 and "became statutory on 29 June 2026" [6], with schools to follow it from 1 September 2026. So for the whole period in which England was described internationally as having banned phones in schools, it had guidance that schools were expected but not legally obliged to follow. And in practice the norm preceded the guidance: by the time the 2024 guidance appeared, evidence suggested "90% of schools already had a prohibited phone policy in place" [17]. England is therefore a case of formalising an existing practice, not of introducing a new one — which is precisely the condition under which a policy evaluation should expect to find small effects.

**The Netherlands.** Dutch policy began in January 2024 for secondary education and was extended to primary education from the 2024/2025 school year [2]. It is not legislation. It is a set of national agreements between government and education organisations, and "it is up to the individual education institutions to provide concrete rules and to determine what the policy will look like in practice" [2]. Schools set their own exceptions for educational and medical use, and some went further than required, banning phones for the whole school day including lunch breaks [2]. The Dutch case is the clearest example of a policy whose actual content varies school by school — which is why its evaluation is a survey of school leaders rather than a measurement of a uniform treatment.

**Australia.** New South Wales moved first among the large states: its ban in all public high schools took effect at the start of Term 4 2023 (9 October 2023), and it "will apply during class, recess and at lunch", with students still permitted to carry a phone while travelling to and from school [7]. Enforcement was deliberately devolved — "The NSW Department of Education offered schools several options for implementing the mobile phone ban" including phones off and away in bags, lockers, magnetically locked pouches, or collection at the front office, and most schools chose zero- or low-cost options [7]. Victoria had already moved in 2020, and most other Australian states followed through 2023–24, making Australia the most comprehensively covered jurisdiction in the world by late 2025.

**United States.** Florida was the first state with a statewide policy: HB 379, "Technology in K-12 Public Schools", effective 1 July 2023, prohibits wireless communication devices — explicitly "smartphones, earbuds, headphones, and smartwatches" — "at school during instructional time, except when expressly directed by a teacher solely for educational purposes", and requires teachers to designate a storage area [3]. The largest district in the Florida study went further than the statute, requiring devices be "silenced and put away in students’ backpacks or purse during the entire school day while on campus, including lunchtime and transitioning between classes", with confiscation and suspension available after a grace period ending 4 September 2023 [3].

The scale of US adoption is often understated in the debate. By September 2025, "30 states have passed statewide bans or have recommended local districts to enact their own bans or restrictive policies", and nine in ten school districts reported having some form of cellphone policy [3]. Globally, "One-quarter of countries had banned cellphones in schools through a law or policy by 2023, increasing to 31 percent in 2024" [3].

**What this inventory shows.** Three variables separate these policies, and each one changes what an evaluation can detect. *Legal force* runs from Dutch national agreements and pre-2026 English guidance, through Ontario's memorandum under a code of conduct, to Florida's statute. *Time coverage* runs from instructional time only (Ontario secondary, Florida state-wide) to the whole school day including breaks and lunch (England, NSW, the Florida district studied). *Enforcement mechanism* runs from teacher discretion to lockers, locked pouches and confiscation. A study that pools these as "bans" is averaging over treatments that differ in intensity by a factor of two or three, which is the single largest reason the literature's estimates do not agree.

### 2. 2. What have official evaluations measured, and with what designs?

Almost every jurisdiction that has adopted a ban has also published an evaluation, and almost all of those evaluations share a design flaw: they ask the people who enforce the policy whether it worked. The exceptions are two economic studies — one on Florida, one national on pouches — and a set of academic natural experiments. The gap between the official evaluations and the academic ones is where most of the public disagreement comes from.

**The Dutch evaluation: 317 school leaders' impressions.** The Dutch government commissioned a study of the ban introduced in January 2024, and it is the most-cited "evidence" for the policy in Europe. Its method was a survey: "Researchers surveyed 317 secondary school leaders, 313 primary schools and conducted 12 focus groups with teachers, teaching assistants, students and parents. Secondary schools reported that children found it easier to concentrate (75%), the social environment was better (59%) and some said results had improved (28%)" [15]. The primary-school finding was weaker still — phones had not been a large problem there before the ban, so there was little room for improvement.

Read the design carefully. The 28% "results had improved" figure is not a measurement of results; it is the share of school leaders who believed results had improved. It is a self-report from respondents who had publicly committed to implementing the policy, with no comparison group, no baseline, no standardised outcome and no adjustment for the many other things that changed in Dutch schools over the same period. A 75% figure sounds overwhelming until you notice that 75% of headteachers saying concentration improved is fully compatible with no measurable change in any external indicator — and, crucially, with the null results found in designs that did measure outcomes. The Dutch study also cannot distinguish between schools that enforced a strict ban and schools that did nothing beyond announcing one, even though the national agreement left the content of the policy to each institution [2].

**The New South Wales evaluation: principals grading their own policy.** NSW's Centre for Education Statistics and Evaluation surveyed school leaders one year in: "a survey of almost 1,000 public school principals led by the NSW Department of Education’s Centre for Education Statistics and Evaluation found that 95% of principals still supported the ban. Eighty-one per cent said the ban has improved students’ learning, 86% said it has improved socialisation among students and 87% believed students were less distracted in the classroom" [16]. South Australian departmental research released in March 2025 used the same approach with teachers: "70% of teachers reported increased focus and engagement during learning time and 64% of teachers reported “a lower frequency of critical incidents” at school as a result of device use" [16].

Three problems compound here. The respondents are the policy's implementers, so the measure is satisfaction with their own decision. The outcome is a belief, not a measure — principals saying the ban improved learning is not a learning outcome. And there is no counterfactual: 81% of principals believing learning improved is not evidence about what would have happened without the ban, because principals who had spent political capital enforcing an unpopular rule have an obvious stake in it having worked. Neil Selwyn's summary of the methodological problem is the sharpest available: "We need to do a lot better than simply asking principals whether they think students’ learning has improved" [16].

**The one place official data did move.** South Australia's department reported a change in a standard wellbeing measure rather than an opinion: 42% of students reported a strong sense of school belonging in 2025, up from 39% in 2023. The department itself framed this cautiously — the results reflect a range of measures including the phone ban but also a $50 million investment in mental health and learning support — and that framing is correct. A three-point movement in a survey measure, concurrent with a large funded program and a statewide policy, cannot be assigned to the phone ban.

**England: a natural experiment the guidance did not create.** England's case is instructive precisely because the policy was largely declaratory. By the time the Department for Education issued guidance in February 2024, "there was evidence to suggest that 90% of schools already had a prohibited phone policy in place" [17]. That means the English "ban" is best understood as the formalisation of an existing norm, and any evaluation of it is really an evaluation of the last 10% of schools moving into line. This is also why the English academic literature predates the guidance: Beland and Murphy's 2016 study used variation in school-level adoption across the 2000s, not the 2024 policy [10].

**The designs that can bear weight.** Two studies dominate on method.

Figlio and Özek's Florida evaluation (NBER Working Paper 34388) exploits the state's first-in-the-nation statute, comparing a large urban district's outcomes before and after the ban and against unaffected grades and cohorts. It uses administrative test scores and disciplinary records rather than perceptions [3][4].

The national US pouch study (Allcott, Baron, Dee, Duckworth, Gentzkow and Jacob, NBER Working Paper 35132) is the most rigorous design in the field and the one whose method should be the benchmark. It evaluates "one type of restriction—lockable phone pouches—using nationwide data combining a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardized test scores, and school administrative records, along with sales records from the largest pouch provider" [14]. The sample is very large — the study "compared schools that did, and did not, take up these strict phone policies over a three-year period across more than 43,000 middle and high schools nationwide" [18] — and the design is difference-in-differences with a pre-registered analysis: "The study was pre-registered, and the pre-analysis plan is publicly available at OSF" [14]. It also verified that the treatment was real by checking phone activity directly rather than assuming compliance, which almost no other study does.

The results, in the authors' own institution's summary, are deflating: "the policies did reduce usage during the school day but had no major impact on many measures: not on student test scores, attendance, or attention in class—not even on perceived cyberbullying. At least at first, the bans caused disciplinary incidents to rise and student well-being to fall" [18]. Co-author Thomas Dee's framing is worth keeping: "There is clearly justifiable enthusiasm for school phone bans, but it’s important to recognize that building effective, phone-free learning environments does not appear to be a simple or quick fix" [18].

**Why the official evaluations and the academic ones diverge.** The divergence is not a conspiracy and not mainly bias. It is a difference in what is being asked. The official evaluations ask implementers whether the policy feels like it is working, which is a question about enforcement burden and classroom atmosphere, and the answer is consistently yes. The academic studies ask whether external outcomes moved relative to a counterfactual, and the answer is consistently: a little, in some places, on some measures, after a delay. Both can be true at once — teachers may genuinely have less to manage while test scores, attendance and wellbeing do not budge — and the policy debate has suffered from treating the first kind of evidence as if it answered the second kind of question.

### 3. 3. What does the quantitative evidence show about learning and academic achievement?

The achievement literature is the most quantitatively developed part of this field, and it contains one of the sharpest contradictions in education research: the same natural-experiment design, applied to England and to Sweden, produces opposite answers.

**The English result that started it.** Beland and Murphy's study, published in *Labour Economics* in 2016, is the most-cited positive finding and the one that policy documents in several countries lean on. Using variation in when English schools adopted bans, they found that "student performance in high stakes exams significantly increases post ban, by about 0.07 standard deviations on average", and — the detail that made the paper influential — that the increases were driven by the lowest-achieving students [10]. An effect of 0.07 SD is small in absolute terms but, if real and concentrated at the bottom of the distribution, it is the kind of result that looks like a cheap equity intervention. It is worth being precise about what the design measured: school-level policy adoption, dated by survey responses from schools themselves, with before-and-after exam comparisons. It did not measure whether pupils actually stopped using phones.

**The Swedish replication that found nothing.** Kessel, Hardardottir and Tyrefors ran the same design on Swedish data and reported the opposite: "In Sweden, we find no impact of mobile phone bans on student performance and can reject even small-sized gains" [12]. This is not a vague null. Being able to reject even small gains means the Swedish data were precise enough that an English-sized 0.07 SD effect would have shown up. Two explanations compete. One is that the English effect was an artefact — of the survey, the timing, or unobserved school characteristics correlated with banning. The other is that the two countries differ in the counterfactual: Sweden's schools may already have had informal classroom norms strict enough that a formal ban changed little. That second explanation is supported by the authors' own point about identification, that "teachers may in fact already have mobile phone bans in practice in the classroom regardless of school policy" [12]. The two studies are not reconcilable on the current evidence, and the field has not settled which is right.

**Florida: gains that arrive in year two.** Figlio and Özek's evaluation of Florida's statewide ban (NBER Working Paper 34388, October 2025) is the strongest sub-national US evidence. In one large urban district they found test scores rose by "0.6 percentiles" overall, with the ban "increasing spring test scores 1.1 percentiles in the second year relative to the spring test right before the ban took effect", and larger effects "for male students (an effect of 1.4 percentiles on the spring test in the second year) and for students in middle and high schools (1.3 percentiles)" [3]. The timing matters as much as the size: "There were no statistically significant changes in test scores during the first year of the ban, when disciplinary rates were high. During the second year of the ban, in contrast, test scores increased significantly, with positive effects concentrated during the spring semester" [4]. A one-year evaluation of a new ban is therefore likely to find nothing even if the policy works, because the first year is consumed by enforcement disruption. Figlio and Özek also report that the bans significantly reduced student unexcused absences, and suggest this may explain a large fraction of the test score gains [7] — a mechanism claim worth flagging, since it implies the achievement effect runs through attendance and habit rather than through in-class attention.

**The national US pouch study: effects close to zero.** The largest and most methodologically careful study in the field evaluates not statutory bans but lockable phone pouches, using "nationwide data combining a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardized test scores, and school administrative records, along with sales records from the largest pouch provider" (Allcott, Baron, Dee, Duckworth, Gentzkow and Jacob, NBER Working Paper 35132) [14]. Its achievement finding is blunt: "average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero. High schools see modest positive effects, particularly in math, while middle schools see small negative effects" [8]. The precision is the important part. The study can "rule out improvements larger than approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations" over the first three years after adoption [8]. That bound is roughly a tenth the size of the English 0.07 SD estimate and far below the Florida percentile-point gains, so if a Beland-and-Murphy-sized effect existed nationally in the US pouch data, this study would have found it.

What it did find is small and grade-specific: "These differences are larger and statistically significant for math, where adoption in high schools increases student achievement by roughly 0.024 student-level standard deviations", which "corresponds to roughly a 0.9 percentile point increase in the test score distribution" [8]. For scale, the authors note this is about one-fifth the gain associated with a higher value-added teacher. The middle-school effects are negative and about half as large, though the grade-level difference is not statistically significant overall [8].

Crucially, the pouch study does not treat Florida as a contradiction — it treats the two as measuring the same thing at different precision: "The estimated achievement gains are on the order of 0.6 percentile points overall and roughly 0.9 in middle and high schools, similar in magnitude to the 0.9 percentile point effect we estimate for high school math" [8]. That is a defensible reading, but it cuts both ways. If the true effect is around 0.9 percentile points in high-school maths and zero elsewhere, then the honest summary of the achievement evidence is a very small gain, concentrated in one subject at one level — not that bans raise attainment.

**The largest positive estimates.** Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella's study of Galicia, which banned phones in schools in 2015, uses synthetic control and reports effects an order of magnitude larger: after less than three years of the ban, from 2015 to 2017, PISA scores in Galicia improved by around 10 points in maths and 12 points in sciences compared with a synthetic Galicia built to follow the region's pre-ban trend in those scores [11]. Ten PISA points is roughly a tenth of a standard deviation on the PISA scale — larger than the English estimate and vastly larger than the US pouch result. The design is the weak point. A single region, a synthetic comparison built from other regions' trends, and a simultaneous national curriculum context mean many things changed in Galicia between 2015 and 2017 besides phones. I would treat this as the least credible of the large estimates, not because the authors erred but because one treated unit cannot support a causal claim of that size.

**Reading the set together.** Three findings are solid enough to state as findings. First, effects on measured achievement, where designs are strongest, are small: the credible range runs from zero to roughly one percentile point. Second, the gains, where they appear, cluster among lower-achieving, male and middle/high-school students rather than being uniform [10][3]. Third, timing matters — first-year evaluations understate effects because enforcement dominates the first year [4]. Two further claims are *inference*, not finding: that the Swedish null reflects saturated informal norms rather than a false English positive [12], and that attendance is the main channel in Florida [7]. Neither has been tested directly.

What the achievement literature cannot do is separate the mechanisms. A test-score gain could come from more time on task, from a quieter classroom, from better attendance, or from a change in school culture that has nothing to do with phones. None of the studies above isolates which, and the pouch study's near-zero average sits awkwardly with any story in which removing phones from classrooms reliably converts into learning.

### 4. 4. What does the evidence show about attention, distraction and classroom behaviour?

Attention is the outcome everyone assumes a ban will move, and it is the outcome on which the strongest designs have the least to report. The pattern across studies is consistent: teachers and principals report dramatic improvements in focus, and independent measures of attention and classroom behaviour show little or nothing.

**The perception evidence is uniformly positive.** In NSW, 87% of principals "believed students were less distracted in the classroom" [16]. In South Australia, "70% of teachers reported increased focus and engagement during learning time" [16]. In the Netherlands, 75% of secondary school leaders said children found it easier to concentrate [15]. These are not trivial findings — teachers experience the classroom continuously and notice changes that a test score cannot capture — but they are beliefs about a policy held by the people who implemented it, with no baseline and no comparison group.

**The measured evidence is close to null.** The national US pouch study, which tracked phone activity with GPS pings and surveyed teachers nationally, reports an effect on classroom attention of "-0.088 (SE = 0.085), indicating no evidence of changes following adoption" [8]. That confidence interval is wide enough to contain modest improvements, so the honest reading is "no detected change", not "proven no change". But it is not consistent with the near-universal teacher-reported improvements in the official evaluations.

SMART Schools measured classroom disruptiveness directly, using a teacher-reported behaviour measure for each pupil, and found no difference between restrictive and permissive English schools (adjusted mean difference 0.06, 95% CI −0.57 to 0.68) [20]. This is a cross-sectional comparison of 30 schools, so it cannot rule out change within a school over time — but it does undercut the claim that restrictive policies produce visibly calmer classrooms than permissive ones.

The South Australian pre-registered study measured academic engagement — motivation, concentration, achievement and stress — using a validated scale, and found that ban and no-ban school groups "did not differ significantly in terms of problematic phone use, academic engagement, and school belonging" [22]. Its follow-up window was one month, which is short; the authors themselves recommend "further evaluation with more sensitive methodologies".

**Discipline: the one place a ban reliably moves a number, in the wrong direction at first.** The pouch study's clearest behavioural finding is that adopting a ban increases recorded disciplinary incidents: "Adoption increases the disciplinary index by 0.057 (SE = 0.023) school-level standard deviations, corresponding to approximately 0.02 student-level standard deviations" [8]. In plain terms, the policy creates a new category of infraction — phone use — and schools begin recording it. Figlio and Özek's Florida evaluation found the same pattern, noting that the first year of the ban was one "when disciplinary rates were high" and test-score effects were absent [4]. The pouch study's event-study evidence shows this spike concentrated in the adoption year and fading toward zero or below by the second year after adoption.

That is an important and under-appreciated finding for anyone designing a policy: enforcement cost is front-loaded. A school that abandons a ban after one difficult year has paid the entire transition cost and captured none of the benefit, if the benefit exists.

**What attention research outside schools adds, and why it does not transfer.** The laboratory literature on phones and attention is real but weaker than it is usually made to sound, and Chris's own *Exocrasis* paper already records the key correction: the famous finding that the mere presence of one's own smartphone reduces working memory capacity failed a pre-registered direct replication, and the largest meta-analysis found no effect of mere presence at all. Nothing in the school-ban literature overturns that. The plausible mechanism for a school ban is not that a dormant phone drains capacity by sitting there, but that a phone which buzzes, gets checked and is negotiated over fragments instruction. Those are different claims, and only the second is a reason to ban.

The best evidence that the second claim is real but small comes from the pouch study's own treatment check: adoption cut in-school phone activity substantially, and teacher-reported in-class personal phone use fell from 61% to 13% [8]. So the mechanism was engaged — phones really did leave the classroom — and measured attention still did not move detectably. That combination is the central puzzle of this literature, and it has two candidate explanations. Either attention measures are too coarse to detect what teachers see, or the classroom was already functioning well enough that removing phones did not change learning-relevant attention. The evidence cannot yet distinguish them.

**Inference, labelled as such:** the divergence between teacher reports and measured attention is most likely a reference-point effect. Teachers compare a phone-free classroom with the recent past and notice the absence of a chronic irritant; standardised attention and behaviour measures compare pupils with other pupils and find them much the same. Both observations can be accurate. What follows is that a headline figure of 87% of principals reporting less distraction should never be reported as if it were a finding about attention.

### 5. 5. What does the evidence show about bullying, social relationships and mental health?

Mental health and bullying are the outcomes the policy is most often justified by and the outcomes where the evidence is most consistently null. This is the section where the gap between political claim and measured result is widest.

**The English cross-sectional evidence.** SMART Schools recruited 1,227 pupils aged 12–15 from 30 English secondary schools, 20 with restrictive and 10 with permissive phone policies, matched by propensity score on school characteristics. The primary outcome was mental wellbeing on the Warwick–Edinburgh scale. The result: "Mean WEMWBS score was 47 (SD = 9) with no evidence of a difference between groups (adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62)" [20]. The study was powered to detect a 3-point difference — the accepted minimum clinically important difference — and the confidence interval excludes it comfortably. Anxiety, depression, problematic social media use, sleep duration and efficiency, physical activity, attainment in English and maths, and classroom disruptiveness all showed no significant difference [20].

The authors' explanation is the most important mechanism finding in the whole literature: "Adolescents attending schools with restrictive, compared to permissive policies had lower phone (adjusted mean difference −0.67 h, 95% CI −0.92 to −0.43, p = 0.00024) and social media time (adjusted mean difference −0.54 h, 95% CI −0.74 to −0.36, p = 0.00018) during school time, but there was no evidence for differences when comparing usage time on weekdays or weekends" [20]. In other words, restrictive policies displace phone use into the rest of the day rather than reducing it. The study's conclusion is unambiguous: "This study does not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form" [20].

The design limit matters: this is cross-sectional. It compares schools that differ in policy but may differ in other unmeasured ways, and it cannot observe what happened when a school changed policy. Its strength is the representative sample — the 30 schools did not differ considerably from the 1,341 in the sampling frame — and the individual-level measurement.

**Iceland: the strongest mental health design, and the same answer.** Bonilla Aparicio and colleagues used the nationwide Youth in Iceland survey across three waves (February 2016, February 2018, November 2023) in a difference-in-differences design across 70 schools, 22 of which adopted bans between 2018 and 2023. The sample is 23,938 adolescent observations, representing 56.8% to 61.9% of the adolescent population in Iceland — as close to a population census as this literature gets. Outcomes were measured with established instruments: the SCL-90-R depression, anxiety and hostility subscales, the Short Warwick–Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale, a perceived peer support scale, and items on in-person bullying and cyberbullying [21].

The findings: "In the postpolicy period from 2018 to 2023, schoolwide mobile phone bans were not associated with meaningful changes in depressive symptoms (β, 0.65 [95% CI, 0.01-1.30]), anxiety (β, 0.21 [95% CI, −0.08 to 0.50]), hostility (β, 0.23 [95% CI, −0.12 to 0.59]), and mental well-being (β, −0.52 [95% CI, −1.08 to 0.03])" [21]. Bullying outcomes were no different: "Results were similar in gender-stratified analyses and for the secondary outcomes" [21]. Note that the depression coefficient runs in the adverse direction and its interval just excludes zero at the conventional 5% level — but the study applied a Bonferroni correction across 11 outcomes in three samples, setting significance at p < .002, so this does not survive correction and should not be read as evidence that bans worsen depression [21].

The Icelandic authors are candid about the limitation that matters most for any difference-in-differences design: "Although there was no consistent pattern of prepolicy divergence across outcomes, differential prepolicy trends were observed for several outcomes, which warrant cautious interpretation of the postpolicy estimates" [21]. Specifically, girls in schools that later adopted bans were already improving faster on depressive symptoms and wellbeing before the ban. That pre-trend works against finding a benefit, and it means the nulls should be read as "no evidence of effect" rather than "precisely estimated zero".

**The US pouch study: nulls on bullying, and a wellbeing dip that recovers.** The national study's bullying measure is a perception item — students' perceived likelihood of online bullying — and the estimate is "-0.039 (SE = 0.092), which is small and not statistically significant" [8]. Its wellbeing finding is more interesting than a simple null. In the adoption year, subjective wellbeing fell sharply, "by approximately 0.603 school-level standard deviations", and then recovered, "becoming positive and statistically significant by t + 2 (approximately 0.485 standard deviations)" [14]. The pooled average across the period is negative, but the trajectory is a dip and recovery — consistent with a transition cost followed by genuine improvement. This is the single most encouraging result in the literature for ban advocates, and also the most fragile: it rests on an event-study pattern with imperfect pre-trends, and it took three years to appear.

**South Australia: a pre-registered natural experiment that found nothing.** King and colleagues exploited the phased rollout of South Australia's 2023 ban to run a 2 (ban vs no ban) × 2 (baseline vs one-month follow-up) design across five public secondary schools, with 1,282 students at baseline and 1,256 at follow-up, pre-registered on OSF. "Linear mixed models indicated that ban and no ban school groups did not differ significantly in terms of problematic phone use, academic engagement, and school belonging. There was slightly higher bullying in the ban group but bullying decreased significantly in both groups" [22]. Their interpretation is worth quoting because it names the mechanism problem precisely: "Imposing access restrictions may not affect the underlying psychological mechanisms that drive problematic phone use" [22]. The study also found that only 2.6% of the sample met its threshold for problematic phone use — a base rate so low that a ban had little room to reduce it.

**The positive findings, and how much weight they bear.** Two studies report benefits, and both are worth taking seriously without over-reading.

A smaller South Australian study, reported in the Icelandic paper's review, "reported small but significant reductions in psychological distress, including symptoms of depression and anxiety, and in negative affect" [21]. This is the finding most often cited in Australian policy material and it conflicts with King et al.'s null in the same jurisdiction in the same year — a direct disagreement between two studies of one policy. The most likely reconciliation is design and outcome: different schools, different measures (distress and affect rather than wellbeing and bullying), and possibly different follow-up windows. I would weight King et al. more heavily because it was pre-registered, published with its measures specified in advance, and reported its compliance data; but neither study is large, and the disagreement is unresolved.

The Norwegian evidence is the strongest positive result in the field. Abrahamsson's study, published in the *Journal of Human Resources* in 2026, "reported that smartphone bans were associated with reduced bullying, reduced mental health care use among girls, and some improvements in girls’ academic outcomes, particularly among those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds" [21]. Two features make this more credible than the Australian positive findings: mental health care use is an administrative outcome rather than a self-report, and the effects are concentrated in a pre-specified subgroup rather than spread thinly across all outcomes. The convergence of bullying reduction with reduced care use is also internally coherent in a way that scattered significant results usually are not. I have not been able to read the paper itself in this pass, so its identification strategy, sample and magnitudes remain unverified here — that is a real limit on how far I would lean on it.

**Bullying: what the estimates actually say.** The two strongest studies with bullying measures — the US pouch study and the Icelandic DiD — both find nothing, on different measures (perceived online bullying; in-person teasing and harm plus cyberbullying) in different countries [8][21]. King et al. found bullying falling in both ban and no-ban schools, which is a trend rather than a policy effect [22]. Against this, the Norwegian study finds reduced bullying [21], and Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella's Spanish work is often cited for a 15–18% reduction in reported bullying incidence among 12–17-year-olds after regional bans, though that estimate comes from officially reported cases rather than student self-report and from a single-region design. The honest summary is that bullying is the outcome where a plausible mechanism exists — if harassment happens on phones during school hours, removing phones during school hours should reduce it — and where the best-powered studies nonetheless fail to detect it. One likely reason is that bullying is increasingly displaced to evenings and weekends, which is exactly what SMART Schools found for phone use generally [20].

**Inference, labelled as such:** the pattern across these studies suggests the effect of a school-day ban on mental health is bounded by the share of total phone exposure it removes. SMART Schools puts the displacement at close to 100%: in-school reductions of about 40 minutes and 30 minutes of social media, against 4–6 hours of daily phone use, leaving total daily use unchanged [20][17]. If that is right, then a ban cannot plausibly move population-level adolescent mental health, because the exposure it addresses is a small fraction of the exposure associated with the outcome. That argument is an inference from the dose data, not a finding, but it is the most coherent explanation of why jurisdictions with quite different policies keep producing the same null.

### 6. 6. How strong is the evidence overall — designs, biases, compliance and disagreement?

The evidence on school phone bans is not thin in the way it was in 2020. It is now abundant, and it is contradictory in a specific and diagnosable way. The contradictions are not random noise; they follow from four identifiable problems, in ascending order of importance.

**Problem one: no randomised trials, and none likely.** Campbell and colleagues' PRISMA scoping review of 22 studies is blunt: "We found an absence of randomized controlled trials with evidence resting on a small number of studies with different designs, samples, operational definitions of mobile phone bans (i.e. partial, or complete bans) and outcome measures, making reconciliation of findings challenging" [13]. The LSE/5Rights review of reviews, by Rahali, Kidron and Livingstone, is blunter still about what this cost them: "The gold standard would have been to conduct a systematic evidence review, but the considerable time required would have mitigated against informing policymakers in a timely manner on a live issue and, importantly, insufficient sources met the quality threshold for inclusion" [9]. When a team of reviewers cannot assemble enough quality studies to conduct a systematic review at all, that is a statement about the field, not about their diligence. They add that despite considerable media attention, remarkably few studies have examined the effects of school smartphone policies on students' academic performance or other outcomes [9], and that "the results are mixed, with methods being contested and some studies showing no benefits or even harmful effects" [9].

Randomisation is not going to happen here, and it should not. Randomly assigning schools to a phone ban is politically and ethically difficult, and the treatment is not blindable. The realistic ceiling is well-designed quasi-experiments, which is what the best current work is.

**Problem two: "ban" names at least three different treatments.** As section 1 set out, the policies differ in legal force, time coverage and enforcement. The LSE review names the consequence directly: "the absence of longitudinal studies, along with differences in research design, sample sizes and operationalisation, and the differing nature of school policies, made it difficult to systematically review the evidence in any meaningful way" [9]. A meta-analysis that pools a Dutch national agreement, an Ontario memorandum covering instructional time, and a locked-pouch regime covering the whole day is averaging over treatments that differ substantially in dose. The most useful thing the field could do is stop using the word "ban" without specifying the three dimensions.

**Problem three: compliance and the counterfactual.** This is where the achievement literature's contradiction is sharpest. Kessel, Hardardottir and Tyrefors replicated Beland and Murphy's design on Swedish data and got nothing, and their explanation of why is the key methodological point: "teachers may in fact already have mobile phone bans in practice in the classroom regardless of school policy" [12]. If the counterfactual school already has an informal norm, a formal policy changes little, and the estimated effect of the policy is near zero even if the effect of no phones at all would be large. The same logic explains England: by the time the government issued guidance, roughly 90% of schools already had a restrictive policy [17], and in SMART Schools' sampling frame only 96 of 1,341 schools had permissive policies [20]. England's "ban" is a policy change for a tenth of schools.

The Swedish replication also exposes a measurement trade-off that runs through the whole field. Beland and Murphy's study rested on a school survey with a 21% response rate; Kessel et al. achieved "a response rate of approximately 75 % compared to 21 % in B&M" by simplifying the survey — at the cost of less detail on compliance and ban strength [12]. Neither study has both a representative sample and a rich measure of what schools actually did. That trade-off has not been resolved.

The US pouch study is the only one that measures the treatment directly rather than assuming it. It verified adoption against vendor sales records and GPS pings, and found the treatment was real and substantial — in-class personal phone use fell from 61% to 13% [8] — and that most adopters were tightening from a weaker prior regime, with "Roughly 62 percent of adopters previously operated under a “no-show” regime" and "An additional 23 percent report having had no formal phone policy at all" [8]. So its null results cannot be dismissed as a failed manipulation. This is the single most important reason to weight it heavily.

**Problem four: outcome measurement, and who is doing the measuring.** The official evaluations measure beliefs; the academic studies measure outcomes. Where both exist for the same policy, they disagree systematically — near-universal principal and teacher reports of improvement against null or tiny measured effects [16][15][8][20]. Selwyn's critique names the problem and the remedy: "We need to do a lot better than simply asking principals whether they think students’ learning has improved." [16] He also notes that Australian bans were not set up "with the intention of properly testing their effectiveness" and that concrete research is "inconclusive, and … not particularly rigorous" [16] — a fair description of a policy rollout that preceded its evaluation rather than the reverse.

**The disagreement that matters most: Beland and Murphy versus Kessel et al.** This is the field's central unresolved conflict. Beland and Murphy found exam gains of about 0.07 SD concentrated among low achievers [10]; Kessel et al. found "no impact of mobile phone bans on student performance" in Sweden and could "reject even small-sized gains" [12]. These cannot both be right as general statements about phone bans. The most credible reading is that both are internally valid estimates of different local parameters: the English effect may be real where bans were novel and enforcement changed behaviour, and the Swedish null real where bans codified existing practice. That reading is an inference, not a finding — neither paper tests it. Its practical implication is uncomfortable for policy: the effect of a ban depends on what schools were already doing, which means the jurisdictions now adopting bans (after a decade of informal restriction) are precisely the ones least likely to see the gains the early literature promised.

**Where the balance of evidence sits.** If I weight by design rather than by count, the ranking is clear. The national US pouch study is strongest: pre-registered, very large, treatment verified, multiple administrative outcomes, published with its own pre-trend diagnostics. The Icelandic DiD is next: population-scale, multiple waves, validated instruments, Bonferroni-corrected, though with acknowledged pre-trend problems [21]. SMART Schools is third: representative, individual-level, well-powered for its primary outcome, but cross-sectional [20]. Figlio and Özek's Florida study is strong on identification for achievement and attendance but single-district in its outcome data [3]. King et al. is small but pre-registered and transparent about compliance [22]. Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella's Galicia study has the largest estimates and the weakest design [11]. The official departmental surveys are not evidence about effects at all.

One finding deserves separate mention because it cuts against the achievement story: the pouch study found attendance unchanged, with an estimate that "allows us to rule out even modest improvements relative to the mean" [8]. Figlio and Özek had suggested attendance as a channel for Florida's test-score gains [3]. Two well-identified studies disagree about whether bans raise attendance, and the better-powered one says no. That is a live contradiction, and it matters because attendance is the mechanism most amenable to policy.

**One more caution about cross-country correlations.** The OECD's PISA 2022 analysis of nearly 700,000 students in more than 80 countries found that countries with a higher proportion of schools with phone bans had *lower* PISA scores [19]. This is a cross-sectional association and should not be read causally in either direction — countries banning phones may be countries with worse classroom discipline, or with more developed policy responses to a recognised problem. It is worth stating only because it is routinely omitted from policy advocacy that cites PISA for other purposes, and because it demonstrates that at the country level, the naive correlation runs the wrong way.

**Overall verdict.** The evidence is strong enough to support three conclusions and not strong enough to support the rest. It is strong enough to say that bans reliably reduce in-school phone use; that they do not reliably improve measured achievement, attention, bullying or mental health; and that they impose a real transition cost in discipline and short-run wellbeing. It is not strong enough to say bans are useless — the Norwegian results, the pouch study's delayed wellbeing recovery, and the concentration of achievement gains among lower-achieving pupils all point somewhere real. What the literature cannot yet do is tell a school which design, at which age, with which enforcement, will produce which effect.


## Open questions

**No jurisdiction has published an outcome evaluation of its own ban using administrative data.** Ontario has had a restriction since 2019 and a tightened one since September 2024, and I could not find a published evaluation of its effects on achievement, attendance, suspensions or wellbeing in this pass — only the policy document itself [1] and news coverage of enforcement complaints. England's guidance became statutory only in June 2026 [6], so no post-statutory evaluation can yet exist. The Netherlands' evaluation is a survey of school leaders [15]. New South Wales' is a survey of principals [16]. The pattern is consistent: the jurisdictions that legislate most confidently evaluate least rigorously. Anyone wanting to test the claims in this report should start by asking provincial and state education ministries for their internal attendance and suspension series, which almost certainly exist and are almost certainly unpublished.

**The Norwegian result needs verifying.** Abrahamsson's *Journal of Human Resources* paper is the strongest positive finding in the literature — reduced bullying, reduced mental health care use among girls, and academic gains concentrated among lower-SES girls [21] — and I have not been able to read it. Its identification strategy, sample size, effect magnitudes and robustness checks are unverified here, and its conclusions are in tension with the Icelandic and US nulls. Until someone reads it closely, it should be treated as the most promising lead rather than as settled evidence. This is the single most important gap in this report.

**The mechanism question is unresolved, and it is the one that matters.** Why do teachers report dramatic improvements in attention while measured attention does not move? Two explanations survive the evidence: attention measures are too coarse, or the classroom was already functioning well enough that removing phones did not change learning-relevant attention. No study has been designed to distinguish them. A design that could: classroom observation coded blind to policy status, combined with a within-school crossover, in schools moving from permissive to restrictive. Selwyn's call to "go into classrooms" points at the same thing [16], and nobody has funded it at scale.

**Displacement versus reduction is measured once, in one country.** SMART Schools found that in-school reductions of roughly 40 minutes of phone use and 30 minutes of social media were fully offset outside school hours, leaving total daily use unchanged [20][17]. If that holds generally, school bans cannot plausibly affect outcomes driven by total exposure — which would explain the mental health nulls. But it has been measured in one cross-sectional English sample and needs replication with device logs rather than self-report, since self-reported and logged digital media use diverge substantially.

**Nobody has tested the design dimensions against each other.** Section 1 identifies three dimensions on which bans differ — legal force, time coverage, enforcement mechanism — and no study estimates effects separately by all three. The pouch study comes closest by verifying treatment intensity [8], but it studies one mechanism (locked pouches) in one country. Whether a locked pouch outperforms a locker, or a whole-day rule outperforms an instructional-time rule, is unknown and is exactly the question a school deciding what to adopt needs answered.

**Age and subgroup effects are asserted more than estimated.** The achievement gains cluster among lower-achieving pupils [10], male pupils and middle/high-school pupils [3], and the Norwegian mental health gains among lower-SES girls [21]. These subgroup findings come from different studies in different countries using different measures, and none has been pre-registered as a primary subgroup hypothesis in more than one dataset. The claim that bans help disadvantaged pupils most is plausible and repeatedly observed; it is not yet replicated.

**Cost-effectiveness has barely been examined.** Locked pouches cost schools money per pupil per year, and enforcement consumes teacher time. One health-economics analysis of English restrictive policies exists (Perry and colleagues, *BMJ Mental Health*, 2026) but I have not read it in this pass. No study I found weighs the cost of enforcement against the measured benefits, which — given that measured benefits on the strongest designs are close to zero — is the calculation a school board actually needs.

**Coverage thin spots.** I did not read the Beland and Murphy paper in full (only its abstract and the replication's characterisation), nor the Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella paper in full, nor the Abrahamsson paper at all. I did not examine the French 2018 statutory ban, the Spanish regional bans beyond Galicia, or the Israeli and Chilean policies. The bullying literature I could reach is thinner than the mental health literature and rests on heterogeneous measures — perceived likelihood of online bullying [8], PISA bullying items [22], officially reported cases — which are not comparable.

## Beyond this question

Three things follow for anyone working on this.

For **policy design**, the front-loaded cost is the practical lesson. Disciplinary incidents rise in the adoption year and fade [8]; wellbeing dips and recovers [14]; test-score gains in Florida appeared only in year two [4]. A ban evaluated or abandoned after one year will look like a failure whether or not it works. Any jurisdiction announcing a ban should commit to at least a three-year evaluation window and publish the baseline series before enforcement starts.

For **attention research**, the school-ban literature is a natural experiment in what happens when you remove a chronic ambient distractor from a structured environment. The finding that phone use fell from 61% to 13% of classrooms while measured attention did not move [8] is a constraint on any theory that treats phone availability as a primary driver of classroom inattention. It is consistent with Chris's *Exocrasis* argument that the relevant variable is the configuration of the environment rather than the quantity of screen exposure — a phone locked in a pouch changes the environment's affordances without changing the pupil's total exposure [20].

For **anyone citing this literature**, the rule is simple: a percentage of principals or teachers is not an effect size. Where a policy document cites 87% or 75% or 81%, ask what the comparison group was. In every official evaluation in this report, there wasn't one.
