report.title: The Tetrad Tested: What McLuhan's Four Laws Actually Claimed, What Scholars Did With Them, and Whether Anyone Has Tried to Check
report.body:
## TL;DR

*Laws of Media* (1988) claims that every artefact, from a zipper to a law of physics, has exactly four simultaneous effects — it enhances something, obsolesces something, retrieves an older ground, and reverses into something else when pushed to its limit — and that these four are derived from the figure/ground and morphology/metamorphosis dualisms, not merely observed [5][6][9]. The book presents them as falsifiable science, but McLuhan's own reply to his first serious critic abandoned the scientific frame for an "analogical" one, and the framework's defenders have largely followed him, recasting the tetrad as a heuristic or a formal ontology rather than a hypothesis [2][3][10]. Scholarship since 1988 has extended the tetrad in three directions — Levinson's diachronic "tetrad wheels," Harman's metaphysical derivation of why there must be four, and a large descriptive literature applying it to digital media — while critics charge that it is too vague to be falsified and too rigid to be honest [4][9][11]. Nobody has published a direct empirical test. The authors ran their own twelve-year search for a counterexample and reported none [9]; the applied literature concedes that two analysts applying the tetrad to the same object will not produce equal tetrads [11]; and no study has reported independent coders, pre-registered predictions, or a single case in which a quadrant failed.

## Key Findings

- **The four laws are four questions applied to any artefact whatsoever.** The canonical wording in *Laws of Media* asks what an artefact enhances or accelerates, what it obsolesces, what earlier ground it retrieves, and what it reverses into at its limit, and states that these "can be asked concerning a wastebasket, a painting, a steamroller, or a zipper" [5]. The preface claims that every product of human effort manifests the same four dimensions [6].
- **The claim is a completeness claim, and the authors treated it as falsifiable.** They wrote that if one question were eliminated and the tetrad reduced to a triad, "we have merely Old Science tricked out in new clothes" [9], and they published the search: "Over more than twelve years of constant investigation, alone and with the help of colleagues, we have been unable to find a fifth question that applies to all media or to locate a single instance in which one of the four is clearly absent or irrelevant" [9].
- **The book explicitly claimed scientific status.** Its opening offers observations "in testable and falsifiable form (the criteria of scientific laws)" [10], and McLuhan introduced the laws in *Technology and Culture* in 1975 hoping readers might enjoy and profit from attempting to disprove his ‘laws’ [1].
- **When a critic took the invitation seriously, McLuhan withdrew the scientific frame.** William Henry Venable argued in 1976 that the four terms presuppose past and present technologists aiming at the same target, an error Derek de Solla Price had warned against [1]. McLuhan replied that the tetrads are analogical — "there are no connections between any of them, but there are dynamic ratios" — and that there was "simply no point of contact whatever" between them [2].
- **Levinson's tetrad wheels made the tetrad diachronic, at the cost of prediction.** His reassignment of the four laws to figure and ground positions lets one tetrad rotate into the next, and he accepts the consequence: tetradic analysis may thus be historically descriptive but not predictive [3].
- **Harman supplies the strongest defence of why there must be four.** The tetrad is "not primarily an empirical theory, even if it has empirical applications" [9]; it is generated by two intersecting dualisms, figure/ground and morphology/metamorphosis, which leaves no room for a fifth term [9]. He also extends it beyond the McLuhans, arguing it applies to all entities rather than only human artefacts — contradicting the book, which restricts it to human artefacts and not, for example, to birds' nests [9].
- **Attempts to add a fifth law have not displaced the tetrad.** Zingrone's 1991 proposal of syncretism was absorbed into the enhancement quadrant, since every technology already extends some organ or faculty of the user [9]. A 2022 proposal adds a fifth *question* — what would not have happened had the medium never been developed — framed as enrichment rather than refutation [14].
- **The Procrustean objection is a double bind, not a single complaint.** Tyler argues the tetrad is simultaneously "far too vague" — a sufficiently creative mind can fill any quadrant for any artefact — and "unrelentingly rigid," requiring all four to be filled whether or not evidence exists [4]. He shows the McLuhans giving two incompatible tetrads for wine on one page, and calls the claim to scientific lawhood "preposterous" in the ordinary sense [4].
- **The number four itself has never been grounded to critics' satisfaction.** Fekete's 1988 review called it groundless, a metaphysically privileged structure with no ground given [12]; Harman's derivation is the only sustained answer, and it is philosophical, not empirical [9].
- **Even sympathetic scholars concede the falsifiability problem.** Basbaum notes that the tetrad's testability can be discussed in the same terms Popper used to dismiss psychoanalysis: "it seems to always work" [10].
- **The applied literature is large, descriptive and non-convergent.** A systematic review of Brazilian and Portuguese communication research (2009–2019) found 21 tetrad applications, only five of which reflected on the method at all, and concluded that different researchers will not produce equal tetrads for the same object [11]. A representative smartphone tetrad concedes that interpretation rests on the analyst's own thoughts and perceptions, and its reversal quadrant is explicitly speculative [13].
- **The one place real data met a quadrant, the data were inconclusive.** Tyler tested the obsolescence of television by games against Yee's MMORPG survey — 21.0 hours of play plus 7.7 hours of television against a national average of about 28 — but reported that such data are "unfit to determine causal relationships" and that "None of these studies is by any means conclusive" [4].
- **The closest thing to a test procedure is an internal consistency check.** Lindia and Levinson argue that if a tetrad wheel built from an earlier tetrad fails to generate the next medium's tetrad, either the wheel or the tetrad analysis is falsified [3]. This tests coherence between tetrads, not correspondence with the world.
- **No direct empirical test exists.** No study operationalised the quadrants as measured variables, reported inter-coder agreement, pre-registered a tetrad prediction and scored it, or published a tetrad that failed.

## Details

### 1. What the four laws claim, in the McLuhans' own words: the four questions, simultaneity, figure/ground, and the status the book claims for them

The four laws are usually taught as four questions, and the McLuhans' own canonical wording in *Laws of Media* is worth having in full, because almost every later dispute turns on how broadly the questions are meant to range. The enhancement question asks: "What does the artefact ENHANCE or intensify or make possible or accelerate? This can be asked concerning a wastebasket, a painting, a steamroller, or a zipper, as well as about a proposition in Euclid or a law of physics. It can be asked about any word or phrase in any language" [5]. The obsolescence question asks what is displaced: "If some aspect of a situation is enlarged or enhanced, simultaneously the old condition or un-enhanced situation is displaced thereby. What is pushed aside or OBSOLESCED by the new 'organ'?" [5]. Retrieval asks what older ground is brought back: "What recurrence or RETRIEVAL of earlier actions and services is brought into play simultaneously by the new form? What older, previously obsolesced ground is brought back and inheres in the new form?" [5]. Reversal asks what the form becomes at its limit: "When pushed to the limits of its potential, the new form will tend to reverse what had been its original characteristics. What is the REVERSAL potential of the new form?" [5].

Three features of that wording carry most of the later argumentative weight.

**The scope is deliberately unrestricted.** The examples run from zippers to Euclid's propositions. McLuhan said so explicitly: "Although these are called Laws of the Media, only a few of them deal with communications media narrowly conceived" [2]. He meant by "media" any informational and perceptual ground that "forms our thoughts, structures our experience, and determines our views of the world about us" [2]. The claim of exhaustiveness is put flatly in the book's own preface: "We found that everything man[kind] makes and does, every procedure, every style, every artefact, every poem, song, painting, gimmick, gadget, theory, technology – every product of human effort – manifested the same four dimensions" [6]. A claim that covers every product of human effort is not a hypothesis about a class of things; it is a claim about a category, and that is the hinge on which the scientific-status question turns.

**The four are asserted to be simultaneous, not sequential.** The McLuhans' compressed formulation, quoted from *The Global Village* (1989), holds that the intensification of any human process, artifact or creation will have four consequences at once — it enhances something, obsolesces something, brings something back, and, pushed to the limit, flips into an opposite effect [3]. McLuhan located the method in structuralist synchrony rather than diachrony: "synchrony works on the assumption that all aspects of any form are simultaneously present in any part of it" [2]. This matters for testing. If enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval and reversal all operate at once, there is no predicted temporal order in which an observer could watch for them and be surprised by their sequence.

**The laws are presented as ratios, not as causal statements.** In a 1974 letter to Melvin Kranzberg, McLuhan described how he arrived at them and what he thought he had: "The Laws of the Media have been shaped by studying the effects of media so there is always a hidden ground upon which these effects stand, and against which they bounce. That is to say, the Law of a Medium is a figure interplaying with a ground. As with a wheel and axle, there must be an interval between the two in order for the play to exist" [2]. The metaphor is instructive: a wheel and axle is a relation, not an event. McLuhan said he had "proceeded by induction" [2] from observed effects, which is a claim to have generalised from cases, not a claim to have derived the four from a theory that could fail.

The ontological backing for the four-part structure is stated most openly in the 1977 *Et Cetera* paper, where McLuhan says the laws led him to see that all our artifacts, all our "sensory and motor accessories," are, in fact, words [2], and that all the extensions of man, verbal or non-verbal, hardware or software, are essentially metaphoric in structure and in the plenary sense linguistic [2]. *Laws of Media* closes the loop with a strong claim about what a tetrad is: each tetrad presents, in Gestalt form, the logos or formal structure of its subject, whether hardware or software artefact (p. 229) [3]. On that account a tetrad does not describe an effect that might have been otherwise; it displays the artefact's formal structure. This is the reading that makes the later charge of unfalsifiability almost inevitable, and it is also the reading that Harman and others defend as a virtue rather than a defect.

It is worth separating two things the book claims, because critics often run them together. One is a **completeness claim**: four and only four dimensions, for every artefact. The other is a **content claim**: which particular things fill the quadrants for a given artefact. The completeness claim is what the McLuhans invited readers to break by finding a fifth law, a challenge the later literature records as unmet [3]. The content claim is what fails most visibly in the wine example, where the same authors fill the same quadrants two different ways on one page [4]. Almost every constructive extension since 1988 has worked on the first claim; almost every criticism has used the second.

### 2. The testability claim and its first test: the 1975 Popperian framing, the Venable exchange in Technology and Culture, and what the McLuhans did when challenged

The tetrad did not arrive in 1988 as a settled doctrine. McLuhan published it as a paper first, and the paper is where the testability claim is most explicit and least qualified.

In *Technology and Culture* in 1975, under the title "McLuhan's Laws of the Media," he set out the four laws for a readership of historians of technology, and the framing was Popperian by design. He wrote that he called them laws because they represent, as do scientific ‘laws’, an ordering of thought and experience which has not yet been disproved [1]. He presented them, according to William J. White's account of the exchange, "in the hopes that those who study technology, including historians, philosophers, economists, engineers, and sociologists 'might enjoy and profit from attempting to disprove my "laws"' (p. 74)" [1]. That is a genuine invitation to falsify, and it is the strongest textual basis for treating the tetrad as a scientific hypothesis.

McLuhan later gave his own account of why he had framed it that way. In the 1977 *Et Cetera* paper he wrote that when he came across Popper's principle that a scientific hypothesis is one capable of falsification, he decided to hypothesise the Laws of the Media [3]. Paul Levinson, who knew him, glossed the move in conversation with Matthew Lindia: if the laws of the media are capable of falsification, they cannot do too much damage [3]. That gloss is worth pausing on. It treats falsifiability as a rhetorical shield rather than a research programme — a way of claiming scientific standing while accepting that the content might not survive. Nothing in the record suggests McLuhan ever designed an observation that would have counted against a tetrad.

**The first real test, and what happened.** An engineer and lawyer named William Henry Venable took up the invitation. His reply, "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws," appeared in *Technology and Culture* in 1976, and it made a specific and serious objection rather than a general complaint. White summarises it: "McLuhan's four selected symbols," Venable says, referring to the predicates of his laws, "seem to postulate that past and present technologists were shooting at the same target, that the present shots come closer to the mark (amplifies) or that present improved bows come closer to the mark (obsolesces) and returned to some old bow designs (retrieves), and that there are presently known or past-known shots in the opposite direction (reversal is)." White adds that this struck Venable as the error Derek de Solla Price had identified, "in which all that happens is seen by the historian as leading with a single arrow to the present" (p. 258) [1].

The objection is sharper than it is usually given credit for. Venable is not saying the four categories are badly chosen. He is saying that applying them presupposes a single direction of technological striving, so that "enhancement" and "obsolescence" have a fixed valency across history — and that this smuggles in a teleology that historians of technology had already learned to distrust. White's own reading is that Venable did not contest the fourfold typology at all; at most he suggested the laws be regarded "as a symbolic ordering–law-like in a legal sense, perhaps, rather than a phenomenal one" [1].

**McLuhan's reply.** His published response in *Technology and Culture* (17:2, 1976, p. 263) is the most revealing document in the whole episode, because it abandons the scientific frame rather than defending it. He wrote that Venable had tried to relate his “tetrades”, or laws, to logic, and that the whole point about his tetrads is that they are _ana_logical — that is, there are no connections between any of them, but there are dynamic ratios [2]. He then dismissed the critique entirely: Venable "has not read me at all but has almost at random used my observations as points from which to take off on his own flights. That is, there is no disagreement between Venable and me; there is simply no point of contact whatever" [2]. The rest of the letter turns to Roger Barker's ecological psychology and to a claim that there is "a uniform response of hostility to any study of psychic effects of technology" [2].

Two things about that reply matter for the later debate. First, when a critic took the falsification invitation seriously, McLuhan's answer was that the terms are analogical and unconnected — which is to say, not the kind of thing that could be contradicted. Second, the reply was not composed as a considered public answer. It began as a private letter to Kranzberg dated 22 August 1975, written before Venable's piece appeared; Kranzberg showed Venable's critique to McLuhan in 1975 and deleted the letter's opening paragraph for publication [2]. The letter is therefore an immediate reaction, not a position McLuhan worked out in response to sustained criticism. This is a point where I am going beyond the sources: the record establishes the letter's provenance, and it is my inference that this weakens its standing as McLuhan's settled view of how the laws should be defended. What can be said with the sources is that the two available framings — Popperian hypothesis in 1975, analogical ratio in 1976 — are not compatible, and McLuhan did not reconcile them.

**How the invitation was received.** Lindia and Levinson, writing in *New Explorations*, make the most useful observation about the aftermath: the philosophical evaluation of the tetrads runs askew from McLuhan's 1975 and 1977 appeals to test their validity historically and empirically. They add that for the most part scholars have followed McLuhan’s request, eclipsing the opportunity to test the epistemological and ontological insights implicit in the tetrads [3]. That is a precise description of what happened. The invitation was answered by application, not by testing. Scholars took the four questions and ran them on new media; almost nobody tried to establish conditions under which an answer would count as wrong. The one sustained attempt to treat the laws as testable claims, Venable's, was met with a denial that the laws were the kind of thing that could be tested that way.

### 3. Extensions and applications since 1988: Levinson's tetrad wheels, Logan's laws of new media, media ecology's adoption, Harman's metaphysics, and the digital-media literature

Almost every serious extension since 1988 works on the *structure* of the tetrad rather than on its particular contents, and the extensions fall into three families: making the four laws dynamic over time, defending their necessity philosophically, and using them as a descriptive instrument on digital media.

**Levinson's tetrad wheels.** Paul Levinson organised the 1978 Tetrad Conference at the New School before the book existed, and his contribution was to make the tetrad chain through time. His move was to reassign the four laws to figure and ground positions, treating intensification and retrieval as figures and obsolescence and reversal as grounds [3]. Lindia and Levinson describe the resulting structure as a wheel with pre-ground, pre-figure, post-ground and post-figure positions, so that the reversal of one medium becomes the enhancement of the next, which is then itself reversed. Levinson's radio tetrad is the most-reproduced worked example in the whole literature, and it shows the intended shape of a complete tetrad: radio amplifies the human voice instantly to a mass audience, obsolesces print as a mass medium (we hear of an important event first on radio rather than in a newspaper extra), retrieves the town crier that print had largely obsolesced, and, as acoustic radio, reverses into audio-visual television [11]. The wheel extension also carries a cost, which Levinson accepts: tetradic analysis of culture may be historically descriptive but not predictive [3]. That concession is significant. The 1975 framing invited falsification, and a description of what has already happened cannot be falsified by what happens next. Given your decision to treat the tetrad as a probe, this is the version of the framework most compatible with it — a device for organising a historical account, with the predictive claim explicitly dropped.

**Harman's metaphysical defence.** Graham Harman has done more than anyone to argue that the tetrad's fourness is necessary rather than arbitrary, and his argument is the strongest answer to the charge that McLuhan simply liked the number four. His claim is that "the tetrad is not primarily an empirical theory, even if it has empirical applications" [9]. Its necessity comes from being built on two intersecting dualisms. The first is figure and ground, which yields enhancement and obsolescence as the "morphological" pair: a medium turns some element of ground into figure, and pushes some former figure back into ground. The second is morphology and metamorphosis, which yields retrieval and reversal: retrieval means a former background medium becomes visible as figure, and reversal means an overheated figure flips back into background. On this account there is "no possible room for a fifth term in this structure" [9], and the arbitrariness objection dissolves — not because the four are empirically complete, but because they are the four positions generated by two distinctions.

Harman also pushes the tetrad further than the McLuhans did, and this is where his extension becomes a genuine departure. He argues it should apply to *all* entities, not only human artefacts, and reports that he and Eric McLuhan reached an impasse on the question in correspondence; Harman still holds that the tetrads ought to be interpreted so that they are indifferent as to whether an entity is fabricated by humans or not [7]. That directly contradicts the McLuhans, who wrote that “The tetrad is only applicable to human artefacts, and not, for example, to birds’ nests or spiders’ webs” (p. 127) [9]. Harman's is the more philosophically ambitious position and the less defensible one as a reading of the book. He also proposes a counter-intuitive reading of the quadrants that he says took him two articles to reach: "to enhance something paradoxically means to make it _less_ visible, and to obsolesce something makes it _more_ visible" [7]. If that is right, the McLuhans' own definitions of the two terms are backwards, which is a criticism as much as an extension.

**Frank Zingrone's pentad, and its rejection.** The most direct attempt to extend the tetrad was Frank Zingrone's 1991 proposal of a fifth law. His objection was to the fixity of four: "why four operations? Why this particular four? The annoyance in these questions persists, burns. This is not fourness on the scale of the atomic structure of Beryllium, is it? And why does it matter that there are only four?" [9]. His worry was that "laws, of any sort, delimit," and that a closed set of four plays into accusations of technological determinism [9]. His proposed fifth law was syncretism: technologies usually arise from two earlier technologies fusing into a third. Harman's rebuttal is decisive on the textual point. Zingrone hedges — technologies "usually" pair, there are "many examples" — which is not how a law is stated. Worse, the mechanism he describes is already in the tetrad: Eric McLuhan defines enhancement as the claim that every technology extends or amplifies some organ or faculty of the user, so syncretism is a special case of enhancement, not a new law [9]. Zingrone's pentad has not displaced the tetrad, and the record of the "find a fifth law" challenge is that it remains unmet [3].

**Logan and the figure/ground mapping.** Robert Logan, McLuhan's collaborator, supplied the cleanest statement of how the four quadrants map onto figure and ground, which the applied literature now treats as standard: "The medium that enlarges some human function as well as the subject of the first law is the figure. The medium that suffers obsolescence and the medium that is recovered are the ground. And the new medium originated at the first law is the new figure" [11]. Logan also softens the reversal law in a way that matters for testing. Where the McLuhans said a medium pushed to its limit reverses its original characteristics, Logan's formulation is that it reverses, giving a twist, and becomes a complementary or possibly opposite form [11]. "Complementary or possibly opposite" is a much weaker and much more defensible claim than "opposite," but it also makes the quadrant harder to falsify, because a medium that merely changes shape now counts as a reversal.

**Attempts to give the tetrad hard-science backing.** A distinct strand tries to connect McLuhan to neuroscience rather than to extend the tetrad's logic. Sérgio Roclaw Basbaum's *New Explorations* paper proposes a "triplex isomorphism" between brain, apparatus and experience: "if the medium is the message, then, in some level of description, there should be a triplex isomorphism between medium, experience and its neural basis" [10]. His reason for thinking it testable is that the apparatus is the least plastic of the three terms, so changes in the brain and in experience should be measurable against it. This is a serious attempt, but it is important to be clear about what it is: it tests a *different* claim — that media shape neural structure — and not the tetrad's four-quadrant completeness. Basbaum himself concedes that the tetrad may fail Popper's criterion in the same way Popper dismissed psychoanalysis, because "it seems to always work" [10]. Nothing in his paper reports an experiment.

**The applied literature.** The largest body of work since 1988 is neither philosophical nor experimental; it is descriptive application. A systematic review of tetrad applications in communication research in Brazil and Portugal between 2009 and 2019 located 21 works, applying the tetrad to Facebook, mobile devices and interfaces, cinema, internet memes, educational platforms, newspaper design, drones and a journalistic data-monitoring tool, and to concepts as well as artefacts [11]. The pattern in that literature is consistent: the tetrad is used as a structured prompt for describing a new medium's relations to older ones. Only five of the 21 studies reflected on the tetrad as a method or stated its potentials and limits [11]. The review's own conclusion is the most telling finding in it. Because the researcher's context is itself part of the ground, "even if analyses of the four processes (enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, reversal) are constructed based on the same empirical objects, we will not have, in different researches, equal tetrads" [11]. That is an honest description of what the instrument does, and it is also an admission that inter-analyst agreement is not something the instrument delivers.

### 4. The criticism: the Procrustean charge, the four-causes and derivation objections, the unfalsifiability argument, and how defenders answer

The criticism of the tetrad falls into four kinds, and they are usually run together in a way that obscures which objections are fatal and which are not.

**The Procrustean objection: too loose and too rigid at once.** Tom Tyler's "A Procrustean Probe" (*Game Studies*, 2008) is the most careful statement of the case, and its structure is what makes it strong. Tyler opens with the myth of Procrustes, who stretched short guests and cut down tall ones to fit his bed, and warns that the tetrad is in danger of operating the same way, with empirical details that do not fit being hammered or shorn so that they do. He then shows the McLuhans doing exactly that: on a single page of *Laws of Media* (p. 206) they give two incompatible tetrads for wine, one in which it enhances grape juice and obsolesces commonplace flavours, another in which it enhances food and the occasion and obsolesces inhibition [4].

The objection then splits in two directions, and it is the simultaneity that does the damage. On one side, conceived as a universal scientific method the tetrad is "far too vague: a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for" almost any artefact a wide range of things it might be said to augment, obsolesce, retrieve and reverse into [4]. On the other, the tetrad is "unrelentingly rigid": it requires us to fill the gaps, whether or not the evidence is there [4]. So the same instrument is accused of being unfalsifiable because anything can be stretched to fit, and of doing violence to its subject because every box must be filled. Tyler's verdict on the claim to scientific lawhood is that it is "preposterous" in the ordinary sense of the phrase [4]. His concession is equally clear: the tetrad has its uses, best treated as McLuhan himself often did, as a heuristic device in the form of a set of questions, a probe rather than a law [4].

**The groundlessness of four.** The most serious review objection, raised by John Fekete in 1988, is not that the tetrad is vague but that its cardinality is arbitrary. Guardiani's survey of the reviews summarises it: Fekete's "only objection, and a serious one," concerns the groundlessness of the number four, fixed by the McLuhans as a metaphysically privileged explanatory structure, in effect a figure minus a ground, which he treats as a flaw and a contradiction in their argument [12]. Guardiani concedes the point in passing — the ground of four does not appear to be explained [12]. This objection matters more than the vagueness charge because it attacks the *completeness* claim directly. If four is a preference rather than a necessity, then "we have been unable to find a fifth" is a report about the authors' imagination, not a finding about artefacts. Harman's derivation of the four from two intersecting dualisms is the only sustained attempt in the literature to answer Fekete, and it is a philosophical answer, not an empirical one [9].

**The determinism objection.** The most common charge in the humanities is that treating media as extensions of human faculties ignores social context and denies agency. Guardiani quotes it in its strongest form: "This is a seductive theory. But to see media as extensions of human faculties eludes the way in which all media are rooted in social contexts and therefore denies human agency itself" [12]. The standard media-ecology reply is that the charge confuses efficient with formal causation. Guardiani's own version: if one looks at the pattern of a historical event through the retrieval and reversal laws, understood as formal cause, the understanding gained is greater than from the linear sequence of efficient causes, which tends to freeze an occurrence in its unicity [12]. Harman makes the same move more precisely — the whole point of the tetrad is to return attention to formal causation after the long modern dominance of efficient causation, and nothing in the four laws entails that only one retrieval or reversal is possible [9]. Whether that reply succeeds depends on whether one accepts formal causation as an explanatory category at all, and on that question the two sides simply disagree.

**The unfalsifiability objection, stated by defenders.** The most damaging version of this comes not from a critic but from a sympathetic scholar. Basbaum, writing in *New Explorations*, concedes that it is debatable whether the tetrad satisfies Popper's demands, since its testability can be discussed in the same terms Popper used to dismiss Freudian psychoanalysis: "it seems to always work, so it is not as falsifiable as the McLuhan claim" [10]. That is the whole problem in one sentence. A framework that always works cannot fail, and a framework that cannot fail is not being tested.

**The paradoxes inside the tetrad.** Harman, who is broadly a defender, identifies three internal inconsistencies that are worth separating from the empirical question because no amount of evidence would resolve them. First, the "heat" of media is treated both as a fixed property of certain media and as a continuum along which any medium can be heated. Second, retrieval is treated both as the automatic result of any new medium and as the contingent achievement of artists and visionaries. Third, the realm of content and figure is said to consist of both obsolete clichés and retrieved archetypes [9]. These are contradictions in the definitions, and they compound the vagueness problem: an analyst who is told that retrieval is both automatic and contingent can justify any answer in that quadrant.

**The reception at the time.** Guardiani read about thirty reviews of the book and concluded that "there is hardly a bad review without some useful food for thought" — his own invented maxim, offered to console himself [12]. The reviews are a useful record of how the book landed. The *New York Times* dismissed it: "The socalled tetrads, or four finger exercises, prove nothing" [12]. The *Dalhousie Review* concluded that the promotion of a science of the media was so unconvincing that the book showed why communication study could at best be a limited scientific enterprise in the positivistic sense [12]. The *Montreal Gazette* called the book's progress down its avenue of inquiry faintly ridiculous, like a tapped-out mine shaft [12]. Guardiani rates Fekete's as the balanced review, and notes that what Fekete valued was "a powerful tool for training awareness," whether or not Popper's theory, invoked by the authors to certify it as scientific, would apply [12]. That phrase — invoked to certify — is the most compact description of what happened to the scientific claim in 1988. It functioned as a credential, not as a method.

Two further readings are worth recording because they relocate the book rather than defend it. Weir, in *New Vico Studies* in 1990, described tetrads as encoded etymologies functioning in Vichian historical mode [12] — which is to say, rhetoric rather than empirical science, and a reading that the subtitle *The New Science* invites. Berg's review made the media-ecology objection turned inward: concentrating on the tetrad and its appositional categories takes attention away from the environment in which the artefact exists and interacts [12]. On that view the tetrad, which exists to reveal ground, itself becomes a figure that hides ground.

**The defenders' case, fairly stated.** The strongest defence does not claim that the tetrad is empirical science. It claims that the demand for falsifiability is the wrong demand, because the tetrad is a formal or ontological instrument. On that reading the four laws describe the structure any artefact must have, in the way a grammar describes the structure any sentence must have, and asking for a prediction that would refute it is like asking for a sentence that would refute the distinction between subject and predicate. Harman's derivation of the four from figure/ground and morphology/metamorphosis is the most rigorous version of this argument [9]. Given your decision to treat the tetrad as a probe rather than a law, this is the defensible position — but it should be stated honestly as a retreat from the book's own claim to offer observations "in testable and falsifiable form (the criteria of scientific laws)" [10]. The book made the scientific claim; the defenders mostly do not defend it.

### 5. Empirical testing: has anyone actually tried to test the tetrad, and what do the adjacent empirical literatures (displacement, remediation, retrieval, reversal) actually measure?

The short answer is that nobody has published a direct empirical test of the tetrad, and the reason is not neglect. It is that the framework as stated does not generate the kind of claim that could pass or fail a test, and the literature has largely reorganised itself around that fact. What follows separates four things that are often conflated: the authors' own counterexample search, the one internal consistency check on offer, the applied literature's use of data, and the adjacent empirical fields that could in principle bear on the quadrants.

**The authors' own search for a counterexample.** The McLuhans did not merely invite testing; they report having conducted a specific kind of test themselves, and it is the only one the book describes. Harman quotes them from *Laws of Media* (pp. 7–8): "Over more than twelve years of constant investigation, alone and with the help of colleagues, we have been unable to find a fifth question that applies to all media or to locate a single instance in which one of the four is clearly absent or irrelevant" [9]. They were explicit that the result mattered: "If one question is eliminated, if the tetrad is reduced to a triad, then, as will be discussed, we have merely Old Science tricked out in new clothes, not formal but efficient cause, and familiar Method" [9]. Eric McLuhan told Harman that his father "spent the rest of his life looking for a fifth, if there be one, and simultaneously trying to find a single case in which one of the first four does not apply" [9].

This deserves to be called what it is: a genuine, sustained, published attempt to find a counterexample to the completeness claim. It is the strongest evidence anyone has that the tetrad was treated as falsifiable by its authors. But it is a search conducted by the framework's authors, using their own judgement about what counts as an application, with no protocol for a third party to repeat, and no record of the cases considered and rejected. The relevant comparison is with an unfalsifiable system's characteristic defence: the counterexample search is always conducted in the terms the system supplies. Twelve years of not finding a fifth question is a datum about two scholars' ingenuity, not about artefacts. The literature records the challenge as unmet [3], but unmet by anyone, using the authors' own criterion, is a weak result.

**The one internal consistency check.** Lindia and Levinson propose what is, as far as I can find, the only stated procedure in the literature that could produce a failure. Their tetrad wheel rotates one tetrad into the next, and they argue that the rotation gives a check on both. If a wheel built from an earlier tetrad does not produce the tetrad the next medium actually has, then either the tetrad wheel analysis falsifies the tetrad analysis or the tetrad analysis falsifies the wheel — their own formulation of the bind [3]. This is a coherent falsification structure — a prediction that one tetrad makes about the next — and it is the most promising thing in the literature for anyone who wants to test the framework. Note, though, what it tests: the *consistency* of tetrads with each other, not their correspondence with the world. A set of tetrads could be perfectly consistent and all wrong. And the escape clause in their disjunction — option (2), that we have misunderstood the wheels — is available every time, which is the same self-sealing structure that afflicts the tetrad itself.

**What the applied literature does with data.** The largest body of work applies the tetrad to a medium and asserts four answers. A systematic review of tetrad applications in Brazilian and Portuguese communication research between 2009 and 2019 found 21 works, applying it to Facebook, mobile devices, cinema, internet memes, educational platforms, drones and a journalistic monitoring tool [11]. Only five of the 21 reflected on the tetrad as a method at all [11]. The review's own conclusion is an admission that the instrument does not converge: because the researcher's context is part of the ground, "even if analyses of the four processes (enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, reversal) are constructed based on the same empirical objects, we will not have, in different researches, equal tetrads" [11].

A representative example shows the pattern. Isabelle Adam's peer-reviewed tetrad of the smartphone, published in *Glocality* in 2016, argues that the smartphone enhances the accessibility and convenience of the internet and accelerates real-time communication; obsolesces feature phones, personal computers and home printers; retrieves the camera and the book; and, pushed to its limit, reverses into augmented-reality devices that restrict rather than facilitate human interaction. Her reversal quadrant is explicitly speculative: she calls a device like the already existing GoogleGlass, creating augmented reality, one imaginable “evolvement” of the smartphone [13]. Her conclusion states the tetrad's purpose as allowing one "to reflect the past and to try to predict – or at least speculate – about future developments" [13]. And she concedes the methodological point that decides the empirical question: she writes that multiple interpretations are naturally possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions [13]. That is not a failure of her essay. It is an accurate description of the instrument, and it is fatal to the idea that a tetrad is a test result.

**Tyler's attempt to bring data to a quadrant, and why it does not settle anything.** The most empirically serious applied tetrad in the literature is Tyler's own, and it is worth following because it shows exactly how far the data can take you. For the obsolescence quadrant — do games displace television? — he cites Nick Yee's large MMORPG survey: "MMORPG gamers spend on average 21.0 hours per week playing the game … and spend on average 7.7 hours per week watching TV … The national average for TV watching per week is around 28, which is what the above averages add up to" [4]. The arithmetic is suggestive of pure displacement: the hours come out of television and nowhere else. But Tyler immediately reports the counter-evidence, that the survey data are cross-sectional and "unfit to determine causal relationships" [4], and his verdict on the body of media-use research is flat: "None of these studies is by any means conclusive" [4]. He then does the honest thing and redefines obsolescence as remediation rather than replacement, drawing on Bolter and Grusin, so that television is repurposed rather than killed. That redefinition makes the quadrant consistent with the evidence, and it also makes it unable to fail.

This is the central finding of the whole inquiry, and it is worth stating plainly. Every attempt in the literature to bring evidence to a quadrant ends in one of two ways: the evidence is inconclusive, or the quadrant's definition is widened until the evidence fits. There is no published case in which a quadrant was tested, failed, and abandoned.

**The adjacent empirical fields, and what they could bear on.** The quadrants do have empirical neighbours, and this is where a test could be built if anyone wanted to build one. Enhancement is, in the most general terms, a claim about what a medium makes easier or faster, and that is measurable. Obsolescence is a claim about displacement, and displacement has been studied extensively in media economics and time-use research — the question of whether time with a new medium comes out of an old one or out of sleep, work or socialising is a well-posed empirical question with competing findings. Retrieval is a claim about the return of earlier practices, and it is measurable in principle by tracking the prevalence of the practice before, during and after its supposed obsolescence. Reversal is the hardest, because it is a claim about behaviour at an extreme, and it is the quadrant most often filled with speculation.

I have not been able to read the displacement and time-use literature in full for this report — the search allowance for this message ran out before I could — so what follows is a statement of where the evidence would have to come from rather than a summary of what it shows. What can be said from the sources read is that the tetrad's own applied literature has not used that literature systematically. Tyler is the exception, and his conclusion was that it does not settle the question. Given your decision to treat the tetrad as a probe, the practical implication is that a quadrant is only as good as the displacement or retrieval evidence behind it, and that evidence has to be gathered by ordinary means — longitudinal designs, time diaries, natural experiments — not by asking the four questions.

**The counterfactual fifth question as a test in disguise.** The most recent addition to the framework, by Echelson, Fialka and Logan in *New Explorations* in 2022, is instructive precisely because it is framed as enrichment rather than refutation. They propose adding a question: "what would have happened or not happened if the medium, tool or artifact under scrutiny had not been developed or if it had not occurred to those that developed it" [14]. This is a counterfactual, and counterfactuals are exactly what the enhancement quadrant needs in order to mean anything — Harman's reading of enhancement as something that "silently murders other possible worlds" points the same way. But note what the proposal does not do. It does not treat the tetrad as a hypothesis to be tested; it treats it as a tool to be improved. That is the pattern across the whole literature since 1988: additions are welcomed, refutations are not attempted, and the framework grows by accretion rather than by surviving attempts to break it.

**What nobody has done.** I found no study that operationalised the four quadrants as measurable variables and tested whether the predicted pattern occurred. I found no study that had independent coders apply the tetrad to the same artefact and reported inter-coder agreement — which is the minimum any instrument needs before its outputs can be compared across cases. I found no pre-registered prediction from a tetrad that was later scored. And I found no published case in which an author reported that a tetrad had failed. The absence is consistent across the philosophical literature, the applied literature and the reviews. On the evidence available, the honest summary is that the tetrad has been extensively applied, repeatedly defended, substantially extended, and never tested.

### 6. What would count as a test: what the record and the literature imply about whether the tetrad can be checked at all

Everything above points to a narrower conclusion than "the tetrad is untestable." It is testable in some of its claims and not in others, and the difference is worth stating precisely, because it decides what anyone building on the framework can honestly claim.

**What could be tested, and hasn't been.** Three of the tetrad's commitments are, in principle, empirical.

The **completeness claim** is the most important and the most testable. The McLuhans asserted that no artefact lacks any of the four dimensions, and they treated a single counterexample as decisive: reduce the tetrad to a triad and it is "merely Old Science tricked out in new clothes" [9]. That is a clean falsification condition. The test is straightforward in form: take a sample of artefacts, have independent analysts attempt a tetrad for each, and count the cases where a quadrant cannot be filled with anything defensible. The McLuhans ran a version of this on themselves over twelve years and reported no failures [9]. Nobody has run it with independent analysts, blind to the hypothesis, and published the misses. That is the single most conspicuous gap in the literature.

The **convergence claim** is testable and the applied literature has already effectively refuted it. If the tetrad were an instrument rather than a prompt, two competent analysts applying it to the same artefact should produce substantially overlapping answers. The systematic review says they will not: "even if analyses of the four processes (enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, reversal) are constructed based on the same empirical objects, we will not have, in different researches, equal tetrads" [11]. Adam's essay says the same thing from inside a single application [13]. This is not an accident of method; it follows from the instruction Eric McLuhan gave for filling a quadrant — that all accurate answers are correct, and that when you have one you should ask "what else?" [11]. An instrument designed to generate multiple correct answers cannot converge. Given your decision to treat the tetrad as a probe, this is the finding that matters most: the property that makes the tetrad a good probe is exactly the property that makes it a bad measuring instrument, and no amount of methodological tightening will produce both.

The **individual quadrant claims** are testable one at a time, and this is where the adjacent empirical literature would come in. A claim that a medium obsolesces another is a claim about displacement, which time-use and media-economics research can address. A claim that it retrieves an earlier practice is a claim about the prevalence of that practice over time, which is measurable. A claim about reversal is a claim about behaviour at an extreme, and it is testable only if the extreme is specified in advance and the behaviour is observed rather than imagined. None of the applied tetrads I read did this systematically. Tyler came closest and concluded that the data were inconclusive [4].

**What could not be tested, on any reading.** Two commitments are not empirical at all, and it is a mistake to ask for evidence for them.

The **ontological claim** — that every artefact just *is* a four-part structure, that a tetrad presents in Gestalt form the logos or formal structure of its subject [3] — is a claim about what kind of thing an artefact is. Harman's derivation of the four from figure/ground and morphology/metamorphosis is the right kind of argument for that claim, and it is a philosophical argument, not an experiment [9]. If the four are the four positions generated by two distinctions, then the failure to find a fifth is a fact about the distinctions, not a discovery about media.

The **analogical claim** is even further from testing. McLuhan's 1976 reply to Venable — that the tetrads are analogical, that there are no connections between the terms but only dynamic ratios [2] — places the tetrad in a tradition where the point is the resonance between terms, not their causal connection. Nothing in that tradition can be refuted by an observation, and McLuhan knew it. The move from "attempting to disprove my laws" in 1975 [1] to "there is simply no point of contact whatever" in 1976 [2] is a move out of the space in which testing happens.

**Why the ambiguity is the real problem.** The tetrad's difficulty is not that it is unfalsifiable. Plenty of useful things are. The difficulty is that it claims falsifiability in one register and refuses it in another, and the register shifts depending on who is asking. The book says its observations are offered "in testable and falsifiable form (the criteria of scientific laws)" [10]. The 1975 paper invites readers to try to disprove the laws [1]. The 1976 reply says the terms are analogical and unconnected [2]. Levinson, a defender, concludes that tetradic analysis is descriptive rather than predictive [3]. Basbaum, another sympathetic reader, concedes that the model always works and so probably fails Popper [10]. Five positions, all defensible from the texts, and they cannot all be true at once. A framework that can be read as a falsifiable science, an analogy, a descriptive history and a heuristic is not one thing, and the reason no one has tested it is partly that no one could say which thing they would be testing.

**What a test would look like, if anyone wanted to run one.** Given your decision to treat the tetrad as a probe, the honest research programme is not to try to validate the tetrad as a whole. It is to make its outputs checkable in the way the record already insists on elsewhere. Four things would do it, and none of them is expensive.

First, **fix the artefact and the time before filling the quadrants**, so that the reversal claim is a prediction rather than a retrospective observation. A tetrad written in 2026 about a medium's reversal has a date attached to it and can be scored later. Second, **require evidence or an honest blank for each quadrant** — the discipline Tyler demonstrates when he reports that the displacement data are inconclusive rather than asserting displacement [4]. An empty quadrant is a result; a filled one with nothing behind it is a failure. Third, **have two analysts fill the same tetrad independently and publish the disagreement**, which converts the non-convergence finding from an embarrassment into a measurement. Fourth, **treat rival tetrads as the normal output**, as the McLuhans' own double tetrad for wine inadvertently demonstrates [4]; if two analysts produce different and both defensible tetrads, the difference between them is the finding.

What that programme would produce is not a validation of the four laws. It would produce a body of dated, evidenced, checkable claims about particular media, from which the tetrad's usefulness could be assessed after the fact. That is the only sense in which the tetrad can be tested, and it is a sense its authors did not intend. The 1975 invitation asked readers to disprove the laws. Fifty years later, the more useful question is not whether the four laws are true but whether a tetrad, written down before the fact and held to evidence, predicts anything that a careful observer without the tetrad would have missed.


## Beyond this question

For anyone working with the tetrad — including in this record, where it is used as a probe in work on pricing algorithms, task-and-calendar apps, biofeedback and voice interfaces — three findings change what can honestly be claimed.

**The convergence finding is the operative one.** The systematic review states that different researchers applying the tetrad to the same object will not produce equal tetrads [11], and Eric McLuhan's instruction to ask "what else?" after any correct answer [11] makes that a design feature rather than a defect. So a tetrad in a report is not a measurement and should never be presented as one. It is a structured list of hypotheses, and the evidence for each quadrant has to be gathered separately, by ordinary means.

**The quadrant is the unit of testing, not the tetrad.** The completeness claim can be tested and has not been [9]; the individual quadrant claims can be tested against displacement, time-use and prevalence data and mostly have not been [4]. Given your decision to treat the tetrad as a probe, the practical rule is: a quadrant with a cited observation behind it is worth publishing, a quadrant with a plausible phrase behind it is not, and an empty quadrant is a legitimate result. Tyler's own applied tetrad is the model here — he reported that the displacement studies were inconclusive rather than asserting displacement [4].

**The counterfactual is the most useful addition available.** The 2022 proposal to ask what would not have happened had the medium not been developed [14] turns the enhancement quadrant into something checkable, because it forces the analyst to name what was displaced in possibility rather than only in fact. It is also the closest the literature has come to a genuinely new question since 1988, and it was framed as enrichment, not refutation — which is itself a datum about how this framework is maintained.

## Open questions

**Whether anyone has tested it.** My conclusion that no direct empirical test exists rests on reading the philosophical literature, the applied literature, the review dossier and a systematic review of 21 applications [11], and on finding no counterexample in any of them. It does not rest on an exhaustive search. Two specific leads I could not pursue: Michael Hildebrand's "Screens as human and non-human artefacts: Expanding the McLuhans' tetrad" (2018), which appears to propose a formalised version of the tetrad, and Lance Strate's writings on the tetrad within media ecology, which I found cited but never read. Either could contain a test procedure I have missed. The search service and my page allowance for this message ran out before I could check them, so this is the first thing to close.

**The displacement and time-use literature.** Section 5 says that the obsolescence quadrant has empirical neighbours in media-displacement and time-use research, and that the tetrad's own literature has not used them systematically. I did not read that literature. What I can report is Tyler's use of it — Yee's MMORPG survey showing 21.0 hours of play plus 7.7 hours of television summing to the national television average, and Tyler's own verdict that such data are unfit to determine causal relationships and that none of the studies is conclusive [4]. Whether the displacement literature since then settles the question of whether new media take time from old media, or from sleep, work and socialising, is genuinely open in this report and should be checked before the obsolescence quadrant is used as anything more than a prompt.

**Inter-coder agreement.** I found no study reporting independent coders applying the tetrad to the same artefact and reporting agreement. This is a negative finding from the sources read, not a verified absence, and it is the single most useful thing anyone could add to the literature: it is cheap to run and it would settle the convergence question with a number rather than an inference.

**Whether the fifth law exists.** The record of the challenge is that it is unmet [3], and Zingrone's syncretism was absorbed into enhancement [9]. The 2022 fifth *question* [14] is not a fifth law, and its authors do not claim it is. Whether the completeness claim is true therefore remains exactly where the McLuhans left it: asserted, defended philosophically by Harman [9], and never tested by anyone else.

**The McLuhans' own counterexample search.** They report twelve years of investigation without finding a case where a quadrant was absent [9]. No protocol, sample or rejected case survives in the published record. Whether that search was as thorough as claimed cannot be checked, and the claim should be cited as the authors' report rather than as a finding.

**One problem with the record, for Chris.** In "After the Net Comes Up," the section headed "Details: The Proposal" is a build specification for a software pipeline rather than a Details section answering a research sub-question, and the document carries two separate TL;DR-style summary blocks ("TL;DR" and "Key Findings" in the body, plus the earlier summary at the top). It reads as two reports concatenated. Worth splitting or re-heading, since as it stands the outline promises a tetrad-debate analysis and delivers a build brief.

q: Write an article from the record's research on algorithmic rent-setting software in Canada: what it does, what the record found about its use and its effects on rents, and what remains unproven. Argue from what the documents show, quoting them.

report.title: RealPage and Yardi in Canada: how the rent software works, who used it, and what the closed cases left unmeasured
report.body: Rent-setting software does not need landlords to speak to each other. It collects what each of them knows about their own buildings and sends each of them a price. ## A shared model does the work a meeting used to do competing landlords feed nonpublic, granular lease-transaction data (effective rents, lease terms, occupancy, future availability) into a common algorithm, which returns daily price recommendations; an "auto-accept" function and human "pricing advisors" raise compliance. The allegation appears in the US Justice Department's complaint and in the Canadian statement of claim, and its structure is the point. A landlord who feeds the model never has to learn what a competitor is charging; the model holds the pooled information and hands back a number. The Competition Bureau's position statement also examined special rules that artificially inflate recommendations (e.g., hard price floors, inventory-limiting features), which is a design choice rather than a market outcome. RealPage's own words for the goal, as the forensic study records them, were "driving every possible opportunity to increase price" and, in the company's phrase, "a rising tide raises all ships." Where the software covered most of a market, refusing it was the exception. RealPage's clients comprised nearly 90% of the market for multifamily rental housing units of 50 units or more, and court documents cited landlords accepting the software's pricing recommendations 80–90% of the time. The difference between those two designs decides how far the American case travels. Yardi's defence is that its software reads only the client's own figures and public asking rents, and a California state court accepted it in October 2025. The federal case went the other way at the pleading stage, where a judge declined to dismiss and noted that using "an intermediary, Yardi, to compile their commercially sensitive data... does not preclude the existence of an agreement". The Canadian inquiry closed on adoption, so no Canadian body has had to settle which design it was looking at. ## A Canadian paper trail runs from a 2017 press release to a 2024 job advertisement The earliest hard document is a June 2017 RealPage press release naming GWLRA subsidiary Vertica Resident Services as a YieldStar client reporting "2%–4% revenue outperformance". Read it for what it is: a vendor's sales claim about a customer's revenue, which measures what the landlord kept, not what a tenant paid. Landlords confirmed the rest themselves. GWLRA confirmed to CBC it used YieldStar, then "terminated" it after an internal review (Oct 2024). Tricon Residential told CBC it stopped using YieldStar in summer 2024 and that it "never impacted rents." Woodbourne Capital publicly confirmed YieldStar use; VP Nick Macrae quoted in academic research (August & St-Hilaire) describing optimizing net operating income rather than occupancy. QuadReal left a trace in its own hiring: a 2024 leasing-associate ad instructing staff to conduct monthly market surveys "(updating YieldStar)," documented in peer-reviewed research. Below that rung sits the litigation, and a pleading is not a finding. The class-action allegations were never tested and are now discontinued; naming defendants reflects pleadings, not proven conduct. The claim named RealPage plus 14 landlord/manager groups: QuadReal, Westcorp, FirstService, Associated Property Management (2001), GWLRA, M&R, Rhapsody, Hollyburn, CAPREIT, Dream Unlimited, Woodbourne, RioCan, Choice Properties, and Tricon. Some of those named said plainly that they had not used it; CAPREIT's answer was "We have not, are not, and will never use" YieldStar. A rung lower still is a claim whose source cannot be opened. A reporter was told that Starlight Investments was one of at least 13 companies in Canada with more than $5 billion in revenue that have used the YieldStar software, citing an unnamed market-research database. The study flags it as unverifiable, and a reader should treat the tier as the claim's standing rather than as an accusation. ## The retreat came before anyone counted the rents GWLRA and Tricon stopping is the shape of the whole Canadian story rather than an aside to it. By the time the Bureau finished, adoption "did not reach the anticompetitive thresholds" and had fallen since late 2024. RealPage told CBC its software has never served more than 1% of the rental market in Canada. That figure deserves care, because it comes from the company: The 1% Canadian-penetration figure originates with RealPage and is self-serving, and although the Bureau's finding is consistent with it, the Bureau did not publish a precise share. > **Objection: software used by a sliver of the market cannot have moved rents, so the question is settled** > > Coverage and effect are separate questions, and the low figure answers only the first. It describes how much of the rental market used the software, which is not the same as how much of the market the buildings that used it represented, and it is the vendor's own number rather than a measurement. On rent effects, the Canadian record holds a landlord's assurance that the software "never impacted rents." An assurance is not a measurement either. ## The inquiry ended on a share test, and the statute asks for a handshake The Bureau tested dominance, which has a threshold: A firm generally needs ~50% market share (65% for a group) to prompt a dominance finding — a bar neither vendor met given low Canadian uptake. The closure is narrower than a verdict: The Bureau's closure is a discretionary enforcement decision on present evidence, not a ruling that the software is lawful; it "remains concerned" and can reopen if "new and compelling evidence" emerges. What it wrote on the way out was not reassurance. It issued four diagnostic compliance questions, warning that even anonymized competitor data used in back-end processes can let software "act as a means for competitors to coordinate." The other route carries the structural problem. Sections 45 (criminal conspiracy) and 90.1 (civil agreements) both require an "agreement/arrangement." Neither reaches tacit algorithmic coordination, and conscious parallelism is not illegal in Canada. The Bureau's report on what it heard recorded the same gap: tacit collusion through algorithms typically falls outside existing competition law because the law requires evidence of a 'meeting of the minds.' The amendments that took effect in June 2025 lowered some barriers, but they do not reach genuinely tacit algorithmic coordination — the core enforcement gap survives intact. They did open the Tribunal to private applicants with disgorgement-style monetary awards, which matters because it gives someone other than the Bureau a way to put the question. Nothing about this is confined to housing. The Bureau's discussion paper noted Canada has over 60 companies offering algorithmic pricing services across sectors, and its inquiry into retail-gasoline pricing data remains open, with a court order behind it compelling documents. ## The class action died before the stage where rent evidence appears The private route to the answer was the class action, and it ended early: it was discontinued by court order effective April 1, 2026, before any certification motion. Its theory was that the software was the meeting. RealPage's revenue management system was pleaded as the intermediary through which competitively sensitive information is exchanged... and the enforcer of the agreement between the Defendants. What the American cases had, and Canada never reached, was the connective tissue: The US cases produced internal documents, sworn testimony, and evidence of RealPage-hosted "user group" meetings where competing landlords discussed pricing — a "rim" connecting the spokes that the Canadian plaintiffs never reached discovery to develop. That is the loss, and it is not only a loss of money. The Canadian discontinuance leaves no domestic precedent on whether a shared algorithm constitutes an "agreement." The rent evidence would have come from the same place the US evidence came from, which is the vendor's files and the landlords' internal correspondence, and a case that stops before discovery opens neither. Tenants were left with a running clock: because it was never certified, class members' individual limitation periods (suspended under s.28(1) of the Class Proceedings Act) resumed running on April 1, 2026. ## The American record settles the conduct and leaves the rent unmeasured The number that travels furthest in this story is American and untested. In the US complaint, prosecutors allege one landlord raised rents more than 25% within 11 months of adopting the software. The settlement that followed carried no financial penalty, no admission of wrongdoing, and its terms regulate inputs rather than outcomes: it bars use of competitors' nonpublic data, restricts geographic granularity below the state level, and requires any nonpublic data used to train the algorithm to be at least one year old. The money in the US record is settlement money. Private multidistrict-litigation settlements total nearly US$360 million across two batches: more than US$141.8 million from 26 settlements in October 2025, and then a further $218 million from a second batch. Read the chart for what it can bear. It is a record of what companies chose to pay rather than keep litigating, which is evidence that the cases had weight and no evidence at all about the size of any rent increase. The antitrust chief's summary is a characterisation, not a finding of fact: RealPage was replacing competition with coordination, and renters paid the price. A remedy that forbids a data practice is what a regulator imposes when it can settle the conduct question without ever having to measure the rent. ## Parallel prices are the weakest thing to argue from The obvious next move is to compare rents across separately owned buildings in the same city and look for lockstep increases. The study that examined the idea says why that will not do. Parallel pricing is the expected output of competitive markets, rent-control caps, and shared public benchmarks (Rentals.ca, CMHC). Landlords can converge because they are competing, because a guideline caps them, or because they both read the same published survey. The study's own instruction for what can honestly be shown is narrower: At most, present price-dispersion visualizations as hypothesis-generating, never as proof. Which is why the honest version of this subject has to keep saying what it is not. state plainly that using such software is not illegal in Canada and that the Bureau found no contravention. Adoption of a tool and proof of wrongdoing are different claims, and the record documents the adoption. ## The concentration kept rising while the software withdrew The part of the story that did not move is the market the software was built for. the 25 biggest financial firms held ~340,000 suites in 2021, about 20% of purpose-built multi-family stock, with some estimates of 30% financialized. Revenue management has a specific job in a market shaped like that: Vacancy decontrol — especially in Ontario — creates the unit-turnover incentive that revenue-management software exists to optimize. The study's own summary of the balance is the fairest sentence in it: Algorithmic rent-setting is dangerous in proportion to concentration, and Canadian concentration is high and rising even as YieldStar specifically retreats. ## The gap outlives the retreat, and a case reaching discovery is what would close it Put the pieces in order and the Canadian outcome is strange but coherent. The software was here from 2017. Landlords confirmed using it and then confirmed stopping. The Bureau measured coverage, found it short of its thresholds, and closed. The class action ended before anyone was compelled to produce a file. What is left is a country with documented adoption, a documented retreat, a rising concentration of ownership, and no measurement of what any of it did to rents. What could still produce that measurement sits outside anyone's plan. The Tribunal now takes private applications, so a tenant-side applicant with a theory of the agreement could compel the documents a discontinued class action never reached. The gasoline inquiry will also have to say what an algorithmic agreement is, in a sector where the Bureau already has a court order behind it. Until one of those happens, the honest reading of the Canadian material is that the answer is missing for a reason that will recur. The evidence that would settle the rent question lives in lease-level data and internal correspondence, which only a case reaching discovery can open, while the statute asks for the handshake a shared model exists to remove.
